article_content: The candidate widely expected to replace Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel has withdrawn from consideration. Michele Flournoy, 52, announced her decision on Tuesday, citing family responsibilities. She had been the leading contender for the position of U.S. Defense Secretary during President Obama’s second term. In a letter to the Center for a New American Security—a think tank she co-founded—Flournoy requested that her name be removed from consideration. A source close to her indicated that she had concerns about the scope of authority she would be granted compared to Hagel, whose tenure was marked by perceived deference to White House directives. Flournoy previously served as the Pentagon’s Undersecretary of Defense for Policy during Obama’s first term. After resigning in February 2014 to spend more time with her three children, she returned to the Center for a New American Security. An Oxford graduate and Newton-Tatum scholar at Balliol College, she spent two decades rising through the male-dominated U.S. national security establishment, earning widespread respect from policymakers and military leaders. Her withdrawal underscores the difficulty President Obama faces in identifying a successor acceptable to both the White House and Congress. Hagel, a former Republican senator, resigned under pressure after struggling to assert influence within Obama’s tightly controlled foreign policy circle. Potential successors now include Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson, a former Pentagon general counsel known for overseeing Obama’s immigration executive actions—an initiative facing strong Republican opposition. Nominating Johnson could turn his confirmation hearing into a contentious debate over immigration policy. Other leading candidates are Ashton Carter, former Deputy Secretary of Defense, and Robert Work, current Deputy Secretary of Defense. Both bring deep institutional knowledge but face their own political hurdles. Flournoy’s exit removes the most prominent candidate who might have become the first woman to lead the Pentagon. The White House has declined to comment on the selection process, with National Security Council spokeswoman Bernadette Meehan stating, 'The president is considering a number of well-qualified candidates, but I do not have any personnel announcements at this time.'

article_content: In the 2012–13 academic year, nearly 820,000 international students chose to study in the United States — a record high reflecting growing global demand for American higher education. China led the pack with over 237,000 students, a 29% jump from the previous year, fueled by a rising middle class and widespread confidence in the quality of U.S. universities. Most of these students paid for their education themselves or with family support, injecting an estimated $24 billion annually into the U.S. economy. Other major sources included India, South Korea, Saudi Arabia, and Canada. Saudi Arabia’s numbers climbed 30% to 45,000, largely due to a decade-old government scholarship program. The most popular campuses for international students were the University of Southern California, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Purdue University, New York University, and Columbia University. Meanwhile, around 283,000 American undergraduates studied overseas — up 3% from the prior year and triple the number from two decades ago. Yet, fewer than 10% of U.S. undergraduates ever study abroad. The UK, Italy, Spain, France, and China were the top destinations. Interest in China is growing, partly due to the U.S. State Department’s 100,000 Strong initiative, launched in 2010 to send 100,000 American students there over four years, and the increasing availability of courses taught in English. In 2011–12, nearly 15,000 Americans studied in China — not including those in non-academic programs. Officials emphasize that all forms of international learning, whether short-term or long-term, credit-based or not, hold real value.

article_content: Orlando Sanford International Airport is making another push to join a federal program that lets airports use private security companies instead of TSA agents — but under TSA rules and oversight. The airport first applied last year to participate in the Screening Partnership Program, which Congress created in 2002 to give airports flexibility while keeping federal standards intact. So far, the TSA has turned down the request twice. Larry Dale, the airport’s president and CEO, insists this isn’t about removing TSA — it’s about using a program the agency itself runs. 'We believe in free enterprise and holding people accountable for safety,' he said. The program now includes 16 major airports, such as San Francisco and Kansas City, and just this January, West Yellowstone in Montana became the 17th participant. New legislation passed in February, championed by Rep. John Mica of Florida, aims to streamline the approval process. Under these updated rules, Orlando Sanford has formally requested a reconsideration of its application. The TSA confirms it’s developing procedures to implement the Screening Partnership Program provisions from the FAA Modernization and Reform Act of 2012. Approval is required if security isn’t compromised, costs remain efficient, and passenger screening isn’t negatively affected. In 2011, Orlando Sanford handled approximately 1.6 million travelers, compared to over 35 million at neighboring Orlando International Airport.

article_content: For over 11 years, Toby, a 12-year-old collie, has called Hilbrae Pets Hotel in Telford, Shropshire, his home — not by choice, but because of an intense, unexplained fear of cars. Arriving as a 10-month-old stray in 2013, Toby was expected to find a loving family within weeks. Instead, he remains one of the longest-known residents at the center, far outlasting the UK average adoption wait of just 29 days at places like Battersea Dogs Home. Despite his friendly nature — enjoying walks, chasing balls, and thriving around calm adults — Toby cannot be adopted because he panics at the sight of vehicles. Potential adopters have tried: one family even brought him home, but when they opened the car boot, he fled back to the kennels. Claudia Churchill, who has supervised the center for 22 years, describes Toby as a 'dear soul' and says she 'would love nothing more' than for him to enjoy a quiet retirement in a car-free home. Staff have tried everything to help him overcome his fear, but none have succeeded. To raise awareness, Hilbrae created a Twitter account for Toby — @hilbraetoby — now followed by over 3,000 people. Yet, despite the attention, no one has stepped forward. Toby needs a home without young children, where someone can walk him in daily and keep him away from roads and vehicles. His past remains a mystery, but his need for peace is clear.

article_content: The UK government is considering placing a strict limit on how much it spends on welfare each year — a move that could lead to cuts in popular benefits for pensioners, such as free TV licences, bus passes, and help with heating bills. Although the state pension itself won’t be touched, other extras that many older people rely on could be affected. Iain Duncan Smith, the Work and Pensions Secretary, said nearly all current protections for these benefits will likely need to be dropped to give ministers room to manage the budget. The proposed cap, which would set an annual spending ceiling on benefits (currently around £112 billion), aims to hold ministers accountable if spending goes over budget. But there’s growing unease within the Cabinet: while the Chancellor, George Osborne, wants the burden to fall mainly on working-age claimants, others — including Liberal Democrats and even some Conservative MPs — argue that pensioners shouldn’t bear the cost. Prime Minister David Cameron had promised during the 2010 election not to reduce benefits like winter fuel payments or free travel for seniors, but Duncan Smith now suggests that promise may need revisiting after the next election. Meanwhile, the Treasury has walked back earlier plans to include maternity and paternity pay under the cap, after public outcry. Critics say the government’s message is inconsistent — one day ruling out cuts to pensioner perks, the next suggesting they’re on the table. A government spokesperson clarified that the state pension remains safe and that full details will be laid out in the next manifesto.

article_content: Nominations for the 2023 Game Awards, which honor the year’s most cutting-edge, unique, and story-driven narratives in the gaming industry, were announced on Monday. Leading the pack are the high-fantasy RPG Baldur’s Gate 3 and the recently released meta-horror title Alan Wake 2, each earning eight nominations—including Game of the Year, Best Game Direction, and Best Narrative. Buoyed by the success of The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom and the popularity of its latest release, Super Mario Bros. Wonder, Nintendo is the most nominated publisher this year with 15 nods, followed by Sony Interactive Entertainment/PlayStation with 13 and Xbox (combined with Bethesda and Blizzard) with 10. Epic Games is the most nominated third-party publisher with nine total nominations. Fans can participate in voting through December 6 via The Game Awards’ website and Discord server. Winners will be revealed on December 7 at the Peacock Theater (formerly known as the Microsoft Theater) in Los Angeles and streamed live across more than 30 social platforms and video networks. Full list of nominees includes: Game of the Year: Alan Wake 2 (Remedy Entertainment/Epic Games Publishing), Baldur’s Gate 3 (Larian Studios), Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 (Insomniac Games/SIE), Resident Evil 4 (Capcom), Super Mario Bros. Wonder (Nintendo EPD/Nintendo), The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom (Nintendo EPD/Nintendo). Best Game Direction: Alan Wake 2, Baldur’s Gate 3, Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, Super Mario Bros. Wonder, The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom. Best Adaptation: Castlevania: Nocturne (Powerhouse Animation/Netflix), Gran Turismo (PlayStation Productions/Sony Pictures), The Last of Us (PlayStation Productions/HBO), The Super Mario Bros. Movie (Illumination/Nintendo/Universal Pictures), Twisted Metal (PlayStation Productions/Peacock). Best Narrative: Alan Wake 2, Baldur’s Gate 3, Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty (CD Projekt Red), Final Fantasy XVI (Square Enix), Marvel’s Spider-Man 2. Best Art Direction: Alan Wake 2, Hi-Fi Rush (Tango Gameworks/Bethesda Softworks), Lies of P (Round8 Studio/Neowiz Games), Super Mario Bros. Wonder, The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom. Best Score and Music: Alan Wake 2 (Composer: Petri Alanko), Baldur’s Gate 3 (Composer: Borislav Slavov), Final Fantasy XVI (Composer: Masayoshi Soken), Hi-Fi Rush (Audio Director: Shuichi Kobori), The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom (Nintendo Sound Team). Best Audio Design: Alan Wake 2, Dead Space (Motive Studio/EA), Hi-Fi Rush, Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, Resident Evil 4. Best Performance: Ben Starr (Final Fantasy XVI), Cameron Monaghan (Star Wars Jedi: Survivor), Idris Elba (Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty), Melanie Liburd (Alan Wake 2), Neil Newbon (Baldur’s Gate 3), Yuri Lowenthal (Marvel’s Spider-Man 2). Innovation in Accessibility: Diablo IV (Blizzard Entertainment), Forza Motorsport (Turn 10 Studios/Xbox Game Studios), Hi-Fi Rush, Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, Mortal Kombat 1 (NetherRealm Studios/WB Games), Street Fighter 6 (Capcom). Games for Impact: A Space for the Unbound (Mojiken Studio/Toge Productions/Chorus), Chants of Sennaar (Rundisc/Focus Entertainment), Goodbye Volcano High (KO_OP), Tchia (Awaceb/Kepler Interactive), Terra Nil (Free Lives/Devolver Digital/Netflix), Venba (Visai Games). article_content: A Facebook Marketplace listing in Toronto sought a female roommate to share a master bedroom with one queen-sized bed. The listing, since removed, offered rent at $950 per month. The individual had previously shared the room with a roommate found through Facebook. Anya Ettinger, a Toronto realtor, commented on the listing, saying, 'I think it shows how sad it is here. People are—rightfully so—so committed to staying in the city that there’s a market for stuff like this.' She added that while many respond to such ads with, 'Just don’t rent it,' most people don’t actually have that choice. Cassandra Fafalios, an associate lawyer at Mills & Mills, noted that while most would find such a listing disturbing, its legality is complex. Under Ontario’s Residential Tenancies Act (RTA), protections apply only to direct tenants of landlords—not to individuals sharing space under private roommate agreements. Since the RTA does not define 'occupant' or 'roommate,' those in such arrangements have no formal recourse through the Landlord and Tenant Board.

article_content: In recent years, a quiet literary phenomenon has reshaped tourism in southwest England: German travelers are flocking to Devon and Cornwall, drawn not by historic castles or coastal cliffs alone — but by the gentle, emotionally rich worlds created by author Rosamunde Pilcher. Now 88, Pilcher spent decades writing heartfelt romance novels set in this very region, many originally published under the pen name Jame Fraser. These stories didn’t just find readers — they became television sensations in Germany. Adapted into lush, slow-burning dramas featuring German actors, Pilcher’s tales now draw up to seven million viewers every Sunday night, earning them the nickname 'Germany’s Downton Abbey.' The result? A surge in pilgrimages by fans eager to walk the same lanes, visit the same cottages, and breathe the same sea air that inspired her stories. Tourism officials report a 14% jump in German visitors to Cornwall and Devon in the past year — a dramatic outlier compared to the mere 1% rise in overall German travel to the UK. Local tour operators now offer guided ‘Pilcher trails,’ and it’s common to hear German spoken in seaside towns during summer months. Pilcher herself, who lives in Scotland, told The Daily Telegraph she feels more celebrated abroad than at home — a sentiment she views as a small act of healing after the war. Meanwhile, her publisher, Mills & Boon, continues to thrive globally, releasing over 100 new titles monthly and translating works into 26 languages, with Pilcher remaining one of its most enduring international icons.

article_content: A 48-year-old woman has died after being swept into the ocean while rock fishing with her husband. Her husband contacted police just after 6:30 a.m. on Saturday after noticing she was missing from the rocks at Killalea State Park in Shell Cove, south of Wollongong, New South Wales. Surf Life Saving Australia (SLSA), police marine rescue units, and the Wollongong Ambulance rescue helicopter launched a search for the missing woman. The woman was spotted in the ocean by the helicopter crew and recovered by an SLSA jet boat around 7:30 a.m. She was transported to the Minnamurra boat ramp, where surf lifesavers immediately began CPR before NSW Ambulance paramedics took over. Despite these efforts, she was pronounced dead at the scene. A report is being prepared for the coroner. Police are urging anyone with information about the incident to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

article_content: Human rights activists in Pakistan are calling for the release of Rimsha Masih, a Christian girl accused of burning pages of the Quran. Her bail hearing was postponed until September 1 after a disputed medical report raised questions about her mental capacity. Rimsha, believed to be between 11 and 14 years old and living with Down syndrome, was accused by Muslim neighbors in a village near Islamabad. Reports indicate she has limited education and cognitive abilities, fueling concerns that the charge may be unfounded. Under Pakistan’s strict blasphemy laws, insulting Islam or the Prophet Muhammad can carry the death penalty. While no one has ever been executed under these laws, hundreds have been killed by mobs following unproven accusations. The arrest triggered a mass exodus of Christians from Rimsha’s neighborhood, fearing retaliation. Many say the law is weaponized against religious minorities, often in personal feuds. Rao Abdur Raheem, the lawyer representing the accusers, challenged the validity of the medical evaluation, claiming it was conducted without a court order. He warned that turning the case into a national debate over blasphemy reform could provoke violent backlash. Past tragedies underscore the peril: in 2009, a mob burned 40 homes and a church in Gojra, killing at least seven Christians after rumors of Quran desecration. In 2010, two Christian brothers were shot dead outside a courtroom. In 2011, Governor Salman Taseer was assassinated by his bodyguard for advocating blasphemy law reform, followed by the murder of Minority Affairs Minister Shahbaz Bhatti by the Taliban. Activists like Tahira Abdullah and Xavier William demand justice and protection for Rimsha. 'We want her out of jail — not punished, but protected,' said Abdullah. 'We’re just praying she’s freed soon,' added William. Despite international outcry, the legal system remains slow, and the threat of vigilantism looms large.

article_content: The air in Delhi has become dangerously toxic. Recent measurements show air quality index (AQI) levels soaring past 700 in parts of the Delhi-NCR region — levels comparable to those found in mines or gas chambers. This isn't just unpleasant; it's a direct threat to life, especially for those with respiratory conditions. A perfect storm of factors is to blame: dropping temperatures trap pollutants near the ground, forest fires are burning out of control, fireworks sales have spiked, and vehicle exhaust continues to pour into the atmosphere. The result? A thick, choking haze that makes every breath risky. For people living with asthma or COPD, this isn’t theoretical — it’s daily survival. Pollutants like ozone and microscopic particles inflame airways, trigger severe attacks, and over time, can cause irreversible lung damage or even heart failure. The Asthma & Allergy Foundation of America confirms these effects are real and worsening. Here’s how to protect yourself: If you must go out, wear a properly fitted, clean mask that seals over your nose and mouth. Avoid crowded buses or metros — yes, they’re cheaper, but packed trains mean more exposure. Opt for a private car or taxi if you can afford it. Your lungs are worth the extra cost. Even inside your home, pollution lingers. Cooking fumes, dusty carpets, and poor airflow can turn your sanctuary into a hazard zone. Clean floors and windows weekly. Invest in a good air purifier. Simple habits like steam inhalation — especially with a drop of camphor oil — can clear clogged sinuses and ease breathing. What you eat matters too. Foods rich in natural anti-inflammatory compounds — turmeric, spinach, jaggery, and olives — can help reduce the frequency and severity of asthma flare-ups. Small dietary shifts can make a big difference when the air around you is anything but clean. This crisis demands more than personal fixes. But until systemic change arrives, these steps could mean the difference between breathing easily — and struggling for air.

article_content: Travelers worldwide often struggle with one universal dilemma: returning home with more souvenirs than their suitcase can hold. Should they buy yet another piece of unused luggage—or pay expensive shipping fees? Now, an inventor claims to have a smarter solution: an inflatable suitcase that literally takes off. Meet the Fugu suitcase—a cleverly designed bag that triples its capacity from 40 to 120 liters using a built-in electric pump that plugs into a standard wall outlet. Inspired by Mary Poppins’ magically spacious bag, the Fugu expands vertically by 17 inches (45 cm) thanks to accordion-like side panels. Inflation takes just 20 seconds. Designed to meet carry-on size limits for departure, the Fugu can be checked as regular baggage on the way home—saving both time and money. Made from durable, impact-resistant PVC—the same material used in inflatable boats—it’s built to survive the rigors of baggage handling. Additional features include four 360-degree wheels for effortless maneuvering, optional internal shelves to convert it into a portable storage unit, and even a flat top surface suitable for placing a laptop or makeup mirror. Future upgrades under development include a refrigerated compartment for perishables and an automatic interior light that turns on when opened in the dark. Currently in prototype form, the Fugu is seeking funding via Kickstarter. Industrial designer Isaac Atlas conceived the idea after being forced to buy new luggage mid-trip due to overpacking. Maker Daniel Gindis expects the product to be available for pre-order by December next year—at an estimated price of £190.

article_content: Ahead of this weekend's Premier League action, Sportsmail brings you everything you need to know about every fixture — including team news, provisional squads, betting odds, and Opta statistics. Here's all the essential information for Chelsea's home clash with QPR. Chelsea vs Queens Park Rangers (Stamford Bridge) | Kick-off: Saturday, 3 p.m. Odds (subject to change): Chelsea 1/6, Draw 6/1, QPR 14/1 Referee: Mike Jones | Managers: Jose Mourinho (Chelsea), Harry Redknapp (QPR) Head-to-head league record: Chelsea wins 15, draws 16, QPR wins 13 Chelsea team news: Striker Diego Costa is available for Saturday’s Barclays Premier League clash with QPR after missing four matches with a hamstring injury. Striker Loic Remy (groin) and midfielder John Obi Mikel (foot) remain sidelined, but Ramires has returned from a groin issue to strengthen the midfield. Branislav Ivanovic is eligible following his suspension for his red card at Manchester United, while full-back Cesar Azpilicueta serves the final game of a three-match ban after being sent off at Crystal Palace. Provisional squad: Courtois, Cech, Ivanovic, Luis, Fabregas, Zouma, Ake, Ramires, Oscar, Hazard, Drogba, Schurrle, Salah, Costa, Matic, Willian, Cahill, Terry, Christensen, Boga, Baker, Schwarzer, Solanke. Diego Costa is expected to return to the starting XI for the West London derby. QPR team news: Manager Harry Redknapp may reintroduce misfit midfielder Adel Taarabt for Saturday’s trip to Chelsea after the pair resolved their public disagreement. Redknapp has not ruled out fielding the Morocco international, as Jordon Mutch and Joey Barton remain sidelined with hamstring injuries until next week. Taarabt recently apologized to Redknapp after publicly responding to being labeled 'about three stone overweight.' Provisional squad: Green, McCarthy, Traore, Dunne, Caulker, Yun, Hill, Isla, Henry, Sandro, Fer, Taarabt, Zamora, Vargas, Austin, Phillips, Kranjcar, Murphy, Hoilett. Adel Taarabt could feature for QPR against Chelsea. article_content: The term 'nightmare bacteria' may sound dramatic, but it’s how CDC experts refer to carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE)—a group of superbugs that can kill up to half of those infected. Two years after the CDC first sounded the alarm about CRE’s spread, the threat has resurfaced: seven patients at Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center contracted CRE following routine endoscopic procedures to treat bile duct, gallbladder, or pancreatic conditions. Two of them have died; CRE was a contributing factor, though exact causes remain undisclosed. The hospital is now reaching out to 179 others who underwent similar procedures between October and January, offering at-home screening tests. CRE thrives in healthcare settings, not in public spaces. Unlike airborne illnesses, it spreads through direct contact—touching infected wounds or feces, then touching a vulnerable area like an open incision or medical device. These bacteria, including common gut residents like E. coli and Klebsiella, become dangerous when they move to sterile parts of the body. Some produce an enzyme called KPC that destroys even last-resort antibiotics like carbapenems. First identified in 2001, this resistance mechanism has evolved rapidly. The culprit in the recent outbreak? Duodenoscopes—specialized endoscopes used in ERCP procedures. With intricate designs featuring tiny channels and movable parts, these devices are notoriously hard to fully clean—even when hospitals follow manufacturer instructions. The FDA warns that reprocessing may not eliminate all bacterial traces, putting patients at risk. Though fewer than 100 CRE transmissions via ERCP have been documented in recent years, the potential for harm remains high. Treatment options are limited: some antibiotics still work, but others have no effect. In extreme cases, doctors drain abscesses and rely on supportive care. A few strains are now resistant to every known antibiotic. Experts stress prevention: rigorous hand hygiene, proper sterilization of equipment, avoiding shared rooms with infected patients, and cautioning against unnecessary antibiotic use. Travelers returning from abroad with severe infections should disclose their medical history—some CRE strains are more prevalent overseas. Ultimately, slowing the rise of superbugs requires systemic change in both clinical practice and antibiotic stewardship.

article_content: The evolution of drones continues. The U.S. Naval Research Laboratory announced on Thursday that it successfully launched a drone from a submerged submarine—a first for naval operations. The technology aims to enhance sailors' intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities. Funding for the project came from SwampWorks, an initiative of the Office of Naval Research focused on innovative and cutting-edge technologies. 'Developing disruptive technologies and quickly getting them into the hands of our sailors is what our SwampWorks program is all about,' said Craig A. Hughes, acting director of innovation at the Office of Naval Research. 'This demonstration underscores ONR’s dedication and ability to respond to emerging fleet priorities.' The drone, an unmanned aerial system, was launched from a torpedo tube aboard the USS Providence. It was housed inside a launch vehicle called the Sea Robin, which fit within the torpedo tube. After surfacing, the Sea Robin released the drone, which then took flight using electric fuel cells and streamed live video back to Navy operators for several hours. Unlike many defense projects that take decades to mature, this system went from concept to successful demonstration in just six years. 'This six-year effort represents the best in collaboration between a Navy laboratory and industry to produce a technology that meets the needs of the special operations community,' said Warren Schultz, program developer and manager at the Naval Research Laboratory. 'The creativity and resourcefulness of this unique team of scientists and engineers mark an unprecedented shift in UAV propulsion and launch systems.'

article_content: Streaming giant Netflix is set to launch in Australia and New Zealand in the first half of 2015, according to industry reports. Two of its acquisition executives are traveling to Sydney next week to meet with local distributors to finalize content deals. Launched in the U.S. four years ago, Netflix has grown to 32 million subscribers by offering unlimited access to a curated library of movies and TV shows — including critically acclaimed originals like House of Cards, Orange Is The New Black, and Arrested Development. Although Netflix is not officially available in Australia, an estimated 200,000 Australians currently access the service through virtual private networks (VPNs), masking their location as U.S.-based to pay the $10 monthly subscription. Netflix’s planned Australian entry comes amid concerns over the country’s leading global rate of illegal movie and TV downloads. In fact, Torrent Freak reported that 11.6% of all illegal downloads of Game of Thrones Season 4 — which broke piracy records — originated in Australia, despite its relatively small population. Local alternatives such as Presto, Quickflix, and Ezyflix offer limited comparisons. Presto provides unlimited movie access for $19.99/month but no TV series. Quickflix charges a monthly fee plus extra for new releases. Ezyflix operates on a DVD-by-mail model, delivering four discs per month for the same price Netflix charges for unlimited streaming. Industry insiders believe Netflix’s affordable pricing, broad catalog, and original content could significantly reduce piracy by offering a legal, convenient alternative. The company first explored Australian licensing rights during the Los Angeles Screenings in May.

article_content: Greensboro, North Carolina (CNN) — A former aide to John Edwards testified Thursday that a campaign videographer, Rielle Hunter, told him she and Edwards were deeply in love — a claim Edwards vehemently denied. According to John Davis, Edwards called Hunter 'crazy' and insisted there was no affair. Davis said he believed him at the time. Jurors also heard from Bryan Huffman, an interior designer who delivered over $725,000 in checks from heiress Rachel 'Bunny' Mellon to Edwards’ inner circle. Huffman said he and Mellon believed the funds were meant to support Edwards’ poverty initiative — not to conceal an affair. Mellon, who will turn 102 this August, reportedly considered the federal campaign contribution limits 'a little low,' though she was unaware the money was funding Hunter’s living expenses. Prosecutors allege Edwards violated federal law by accepting nearly $925,000 from Mellon and deceased fundraiser Fred Baron to pay for Hunter’s travel, medical care, and housing during his 2008 presidential bid. The funds were concealed through falsified campaign finance reports. Another former staffer, Mark Kornblau, revealed that Edwards refused in December 2007 to sign a sworn affidavit denying paternity of Hunter’s child — even though signing it might have deterred the National Enquirer from publishing the story. Legal experts noted this refusal signaled Edwards’ awareness that lying under oath carried serious legal risk, unlike public denials. Davis recounted encountering Hunter unexpectedly at a Detroit hotel in February 2007. After a brief elevator encounter, Hunter knocked on his door and declared her romance with Edwards. Davis said he dismissed her claims, saying he was focused solely on the campaign. In another revealing moment, Davis recalled overhearing Edwards on a phone call after a CNN appearance, asking a woman — presumed to be Hunter — 'Can you tell if you are showing?' — suggesting awareness of her pregnancy. Earlier testimony indicated Hunter became pregnant in May 2007. Huffman described the transfer of funds as a 'furniture business': Mellon wrote checks to him for furniture purchases, which he then passed along to Andrew Young’s family. Cheri Young endorsed the checks under her maiden name. She later said she felt 'disgusted' by the arrangement. Edwards’ defense maintains the money was intended to shield his family from scandal, not to fund a campaign. While Edwards admits his conduct was wrong, he insists it was not criminal. The jury must decide whether these actions crossed the line into illegal campaign finance violations.
translated_content: ግሪንስቦሮ, ናርት ካሮሊና (CNN) — የጆን ኢድዋርድስ የቅርብ ሰው አንዱ በአምስተኛ ቀን እንደሚያሳየው የጥቅም አስተዳደር አንድ አገልግሎት ነበረች, ስለ ጆን ኢድዋርድስ እና ራይኤል ሀንተር መካከል ያለው አንድ የእንቅስቃሴ አስተያየት ሲሰማ, እና ጆን ኢድዋርድስ እንዲህ አሉት፦ 'እሷ ተፈጥሮ ነች' እና አንድ አገልግሎት አይነት አይደለም ብለዋል። ዳዊስ በዚያ ጊዜ እንዲያመነዝገው አደረገ። በተጨማሪ የግልጽ አስተዳደር አንድ አስተዳደር በዚያ ቀን ምክር ሆኖ ይቀበላል፦ ራቻል 'ቡኒ' ሜልን ከሚታወቀው አስተዳደር ከአንድ ታላቅ አስተዳደር በ725,000 ዶላር አካባቢ አስተዳደር አደረገች። ሀንፎም እና ሜልን እንደሚያምን የኢድዋርድስ የዝናብ አስተዳደር ለመደገፍ ነበር። ሜልን ከአስራ ሁለት አመታት በላይ ይኖራል እና በ2008 የመርከብ አስተዳደር ላይ የተገለጸው አስመንጫ በአንድ ክፍት እንደተመጣጠነ አለች፣ ነገር ግን የሃንተር ማስታወቂያ ለማስተዋል እንደሚያስፈልገው አልቃለች። የድርጅት ምክር የኢድዋርድስ ከመልን እና ከተሞተ የቴክሳስ አስተዳደር ፍረድ ባሮን በ925,000 ዶላር አስተዳደር አድርጓል፣ ለሃንተር በ2008 የመርከብ እርግጠኝነት ላይ ለማስታወቂያ ለመደገፍ ነበር። የተገለጸው የመርከብ አስተዳደር ስም እንደሚያመለክት አልተገለጸም። በተጨማሪ የቅርብ ሰው ማርክ ኮርንብላው የኢድዋርድስ በዲሴምበር 2007 ላይ የሃንተር ልጅ የሆነ ምናልባት እንደሌለው በአንድ አስተያየት ላይ ምክር አልሰጠውም፣ ነገር ግን በዚያ ጊዜ የናሽናል ኢንቬይሬር ማስታወቂያ እንዲያስከትል እንደሚችል አለች። የቅርብ ሰው አስተያየት እንደሚያሳየው የኢድዋርድስ ምክር የአስተያየት ስም እንደሚያስፈልገው በስም ላይ እንደተስፋ ይታወቃል። ዳዊስ በ2007 ፍብሪያሪ በድetroit እንደ የተወሰነ እንደ ሃንተር በግልጽ የተገናኘ ነበር። በአንድ እlevator ውስጥ በአንድ ርዝመት በኩል ከመቼ በኋላ ሃንተር በመንገድ አስተዳደር አድርጓል። ሃንተር እንደሚያሳየው እና ጆን ኢድዋርድስ በሙሉ በፍቅር ላይ ነው ብለዋል። ዳዊስ እንደሚያሳየው የጥቅም ምክር ለማስተዋል ነበር። በሌላ አስተያየት ዳዊስ ከCNN አስተያየት በኋላ ጆን ኢድዋርድስ በስልክ ላይ እንደሚያሳየው እንደ ሃንተር እንደ እንቅስቃሴ እንደሚያስከትል ተገኘው, 'እንደሚያሳየው እንደ ይታያል?' ብለው አለች። የተቀደመ አስተያየት ሃንተር በ2007 ማይ የተደገፈ ነበር። ሀንፎም የተቀደመው አስተዳደር እንደ 'አየር የተሻሻለ ስራ' ነበር፦ ሜልን በአንድ ስብስብ ላይ አስተዳደር አድርጓል፣ ነገር ግን ሀንፎም የመልስ ስልክ አልሰጠም፣ ነገር ግን በአንድ ልጅ ውስጥ አስተዳደር አድርጓል። ሳንቲ የይንግ አስተዳደር በየትኛውም ስም አድርጓል። እና በኋላ እንደሚያሳየው የተገለጸው በአስተዳደር ላይ የተደገፈ ነበር። የኢድዋርድስ ምክር የአስተዳደሩ አስተዳደር ለመንገድ ለማስተዋል ነበር፣ እና ለእንግዲህ ለማስተዋል አይደለም። ጆን ኢድዋርድስ የተደገፈው እንደ ይታወቃል፣ ነገር ግን የተደገፈው እንደ አይደለም ብለዋል። ምክር እንደ ይታወቃል እንደ ይታወቃል የሚያስፈልግ ነው።

article_content: On Wednesday evening, veteran CBS newsman Bob Simon, 73, died after the taxi he was riding in crashed into a Mercedes-Benz and then a highway median on Manhattan’s West Side. The driver, Abdul Reshad Fedahi, 44, had a long history of traffic violations — including nine license suspensions — and had previously been fired by his company, Skyline Credit Ride. Despite repeated complaints from passengers and fellow drivers about his reckless behavior, management reportedly did nothing beyond checking whether his license was valid. 'If he has a license, he can drive,' one employee told the New York Post. Just two days before the crash, another driver had warned supervisors about Fedahi’s unsafe habits. Fedahi was operating under a less-stringent 'full-hire' permit, meaning he never completed the formal taxi driver training required for medallion drivers. He was leasing the vehicle through Travez Transportation, which has ties to Skyline. Witnesses say Fedahi may have accidentally pressed the accelerator instead of the brake, causing the vehicle to strike the Mercedes, driven by 23-year-old Zachary Miller, before slamming into the barrier. Miller, uninjured, expressed deep sorrow, saying, 'I wish there was anything anyone could’ve done to stop this.' Simon, a Pulitzer-caliber journalist known for covering wars from Vietnam to Iraq, was headed to a lecture on Ebola — a story he was preparing for broadcast. He wasn’t wearing a seatbelt and suffered fatal injuries, including a broken neck. Authorities are reviewing the cab’s black box and have not yet filed charges. Fedahi, who had been living in a homeless shelter on Ward’s Island for months, was seriously injured in the crash and is now recovering at Bellevue Hospital. His cousin says Fedahi struggled deeply after a separation from his wife and attempted suicide years ago by jumping from a building. Though his personal pain is undeniable, the tragedy underscores a broader failure: a system that allowed a repeatedly flagged driver to remain on the road.

article_content: On a quiet morning near Mandera, Kenya, a bus bound for Nairobi was ambushed by heavily armed militants affiliated with Al-Shabaab. After stopping the vehicle with gunfire and a rocket-propelled grenade, the attackers forced all 60 passengers to exit. They then separated them based on religion, requiring individuals to recite passages from the Quran. Those unable to do so — including women and children — were executed at point-blank range. Twenty-eight people died in the attack, while three survived after correctly reciting the verses. The militants fled toward the Somali border after the massacre. Kenyan authorities confirmed the victims included public servants traveling for the Christmas holidays. The attack was claimed by Al-Shabaab as retaliation for recent police raids on mosques in Mombasa, which led to multiple arrests and one fatality. Emergency responders faced delays due to inadequate equipment and slow mobilization, while local police admitted their weapons were outmatched. The bodies were transported to Chiromo Mortuary in Nairobi, where grieving families waited. This incident echoes past atrocities, such as the 2013 Westgate mall siege, where non-Muslims were similarly targeted. Kenya’s military intervention in Somalia since 2011 has fueled ongoing retaliation from the group, despite territorial losses and international pressure. UN experts warn that airstrikes alone have not diminished Al-Shabaab’s capacity to carry out devastating attacks across the region.

article_content: Arsenal and Manchester United have long been among the Premier League’s most storied rivals. Yet in their last 11 meetings, the Gunners have managed just one win — back in 2011. Louis van Gaal will lead his injury-depleted side to the Emirates on Saturday, buoyed by recent momentum: United defeated Arsenal 1-0 at Old Trafford last season and held them to a goalless draw in north London. Aaron Ramsey scored the lone goal in Arsenal’s 1-0 home victory over United in 2011 — their only win in the past decade-plus of clashes. Danny Welbeck, now at Arsenal, netted the decisive goal the last time United won at the Emirates in 2012. Former Arsenal striker Robin van Persie was instrumental in United’s successes, scoring the winner at Old Trafford in the 2022–23 season and again during a 1-1 draw at the Emirates later that year, cancelling out a Theo Walcott strike. In that 2011 win, five members of Arsenal’s starting XI — including Wojciech Szczesny, Laurent Koscielny, Walcott, Ramsey, and Jack Wilshere — still play for the club today. While the fixture once decided league titles, this year’s clash is more likely to determine who claims the final Champions League berth. For Arsenal, hope lies in United’s dismal away record: they have yet to win on the road this season, and haven’t picked up three points away since a 4-0 triumph over Newcastle on April 5, 2023. The Gunners will be desperate to break their losing streak against their oldest rivals.

article_content: Defending motorcycle champion Marc Coma of Spain won Wednesday’s 362-kilometer fourth stage of the Dakar Rally, traveling from San Juan to Chilecito. However, he still trails his KTM teammate Cyril Despres in the overall standings. The 35-year-old finished more than two minutes ahead of Despres on the stage, yet Despres remains 8 minutes and 10 seconds ahead overall. The two are well ahead of their rivals: third-place Helder Rodrigues of Portugal — who finished fourth on the stage — is nearly 27 minutes behind. Coma, who lost 10 minutes on Tuesday after taking a wrong route, told reporters: 'I tried to push hard from the start, but it was difficult. I managed to overtake a few riders and gained some time on Cyril. I’ll keep fighting every day.' Meanwhile, nine-time overall winner Stéphane Peterhansel took the lead in the car category after winning Wednesday’s stage. The 46-year-old Mini driver finished 5 minutes and 19 seconds ahead of Argentina’s Orlando Terranova in a Toyota, with South Africa’s Giniel De Villiers, also in a Toyota, in third. Peterhansel now leads De Villiers by 5 minutes and 41 seconds overall, while defending champion Nasser Al-Attiyah of Qatar has slipped to seventh place after his Hummer suffered a breakdown.

article_content: Engulfed in smoke, sparks, and flames, revelers at the National Pyrotechnic Festival in Tultepec, Mexico, celebrate the town’s deep-rooted fireworks tradition — with little regard for conventional safety standards. Photographed by American artist Thomas Prior, the annual event draws more than 100,000 spectators to the heart of Mexico’s fireworks production hub. The festival, dating back to the mid-19th century, honors Saint John of God, the patron saint of pyrotechnicians. The centerpiece is a lively procession of 'toritos' — bull-shaped frames loaded with fireworks — with around 250 of them racing through the streets. Participants sprint alongside them, often engulfed in fire and smoke. Other major attractions include 'castillos': towering wooden, reed, and paper structures adorned with fireworks that ignite in choreographed patterns, creating dazzling visual displays. Another highlight is the 'pamplonada,' a firework-filled twist on Spain’s Running of the Bulls, featuring brightly painted frames that charge down narrow alleys. Beyond the main events, the festival offers amusement rides, live music, traditional dances, sky lantern releases, and regional cuisine, spread across Tultepec’s town center and the nearby San Antonio Xahuento fairgrounds. Prior, who captured the chaos in stunning detail, remarked: 'It puts our Fourth of July celebrations to shame — but honestly, I’d avoid trying this at home.'

article_content: In a bid to raise educational standards, UK Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg has pushed forward controversial proposals to overhaul how primary school children are assessed. Rather than waiting until age 11, the government wants to begin evaluating pupils as early as age four or five—long before formal exams kick in. The goal? To catch learning gaps early and ensure every child has a solid foundation before entering secondary school. Under the proposed system, 11-year-olds would be grouped into national achievement bands—like the top 10%, middle 50%, or bottom 10%—to provide clearer insight into how individual students compare across the country. Schools failing to get 85% of their pupils ready for secondary-level work by 2016 could face intervention from Ofsted, possibly even conversion into academies. Clegg insists this isn’t about shaming students or turning classrooms into test-prep factories. 'I don’t want my kids to be part of an exam sausage factory,' he said, acknowledging public fears. Instead, he argues that if nearly half of children leave primary school unprepared, the system is broken. 'We’re not trying to celebrate or punish—we’re trying to give teachers and parents honest feedback,' he explained. But educators aren’t convinced. Teaching unions argue that excessive testing distracts from real learning, encourages rote memorization, and burdens teachers with administrative overload. NAHT’s Russell Hobby warned that a single hour-long test can’t capture a child’s full potential, especially when teachers have spent years building nuanced understanding. NUT’s Christine Blower pointed out that hitting the 85% target would require widespread 'teaching to the test'—something she calls unsustainable. Meanwhile, Ofsted’s Sir Michael Wilshaw went further, suggesting children should be screened for basic literacy and numeracy even before starting school. He believes waiting until the end of Reception year is already too late. To help bridge the gap for disadvantaged students, Clegg announced an increase in the pupil premium—from £900 to £1,300 per eligible child starting next year. Critics also highlight the growing burden on children: by age 16, many will have sat four major national exams—and with the new proposal, that number rises to seven within 12 years. While supporters say accountability drives improvement, opponents fear the cost to children’s well-being and creativity may be too high.

article_content: ‘Excuse me,’ the woman asked. ‘Is the president still speaking?’ ‘I think so,’ I replied. She frowned slightly—not out of political frustration, but because her furniture delivery truck was stuck. She stood beside it near the corner of Sherwood and Dawson streets in central Ohio, where President Barack Obama was holding a rally just blocks away at Capital University. The neighborhood was packed with campaign-goers’ cars, blocking access to driveways—including hers. ‘I had this delivery scheduled,’ she said calmly, ‘but I didn’t realize the president would be here today. The guys are trying to find another route to get the furniture to my house. I’m just standing here to keep an eye on it.’ Ohio is a frequent stop for presidential candidates. This summer alone, Paul Ryan visited twice, Mitt Romney at least once, and now Obama had arrived. These scenes replay every four years—especially in battleground states—where it feels odd if you don’t see a motorcade or police escort. Candidates are, in essence, traveling salespeople. They carry their most important product: themselves. Though they’re the most visible figures in American politics, their behavior mirrors that of countless sales reps who knock on doors across the country every week. When you're buying a big-ticket item—a house, a car—you feel like royalty. Agents and dealers are everywhere, eager to please, constantly following up. Once the deal is done? Silence. That’s the rhythm of presidential campaigning: intense, personal attention… until November. Voters in swing states may find this relentless courting flattering—or exhausting—knowing it won’t last. Meanwhile, candidates, exhausted and stretched thin, drive hundreds of miles, believing that face-to-face contact still closes the deal better than any ad or tweet. Because if they’re not there, the other side will be. Watching these candidates move across America, you can’t help but think of Willy Loman—the tragic salesman of Arthur Miller’s 'Death of a Salesman'—‘a man way out there in the blue, riding on a smile and a shoeshine.’ On the day Obama spoke at Capital, the Secret Service blocked Pleasant Ridge Avenue—but let pedestrians pass to grab pizza from the shop next door. A local man, walking with a cane and running for a minor local office, wandered among the diners, handing out flyers: ‘I’d like your vote this fall. I’m on the ballot.’ In less than nine weeks, two of the four major candidates—Obama, Romney, Ryan, Biden—will learn they failed to win. Two will celebrate victory. The uncertainty makes their grand campaign trail feel strangely human, even small. Arthur Miller knew it well: ‘A salesman is got to dream, boy. It comes with the territory.’

article_content: In the summer of 2013, a heated public clash between New Jersey Governor Chris Christie and Kentucky Senator Rand Paul has already set the tone for what many believe will be a fierce 2016 Republican presidential primary. Their disagreement—centered on surveillance, civil rights, and federal spending—isn’t just about policy. It’s a microcosm of the Republican Party’s soul-searching over its identity after two consecutive presidential losses. Christie, a pragmatic establishment figure, criticized Paul’s libertarian stance on government surveillance as reckless, calling it a 'dangerous thought' that undermines national security. Paul fired back, arguing that championing privacy and limiting federal overreach isn’t weakness—it’s how the GOP can attract younger, tech-savvy voters and rebuild its base. Meanwhile, Representative Peter King joined the fray, accusing Paul of wanting to retreat into isolationism, a claim Paul dismissed as misleading. Despite the tension, Paul attempted to de-escalate, inviting Christie for a casual beer near the Senate—anywhere, even Philadelphia—to talk things out. Christie, ever the blunt New Jerseyan, brushed it off: 'I’ve got work to do here.' His refusal to engage personally underscores his political brand: no-nonsense, results-driven, unapologetically direct. Polls from Pew Research reveal the depth of the divide: 54% of Republicans want the party to move further right, while 40% urge moderation. Christie enjoys broader appeal among independents and even some Democrats, whereas Paul leads among conservative Republicans but struggles to cross over. This isn’t just a personality clash—it’s a battle over who gets to define modern conservatism. The 'bacon' comment—Paul’s retort to Christie’s accusation that he hoards federal funds—wasn’t about weight, as some speculated. It was a sharp jab at political hypocrisy: Christie, who secured billions in federal aid for Sandy recovery, calling out Paul for pork-barrel spending. The irony wasn’t lost on observers. As CNN’s John King noted, 'This is just the beginning.' With immigration, taxes, and outreach to Latino voters looming, the fireworks are far from over.

article_content: Police believe the skull and jawbone found on the property of missing 67-year-old Patricia Ritz may be human remains, potentially consumed by her pack of more than 50 wolfdogs after her death. Neighbors reported not seeing Ritz for nearly two weeks, prompting a welfare check on Saturday. Authorities found over 50 malnourished wolfdogs — some confined in cages, others roaming freely — along with several dead animals. Ohio County Coroner Larry Bevil is working to confirm the identity of the remains, but results may take days or weeks. No other human remains have been recovered. Investigators suspect the dogs, deprived of food and water, resorted to scavenging out of survival instinct. 'She really wanted to save them all,' said Tracey Ward of Ohio County Animal Control, explaining the uncontrolled breeding that led to the overwhelming number of animals. Animal Control has since taken custody of the surviving dogs and is working to place them in specialized sanctuaries. Public reaction has ranged from morbid humor to compassion, with many emphasizing that the dogs’ actions were driven by hunger, not malice. Comments also highlighted the tragedy of animal neglect and the difficulty of rehoming hybrid animals raised in such conditions.

article_content: A young woman in Sydney’s Northern Beaches has turned a frustrating road hazard into a viral moment — documenting how a small pothole outside her home expanded dramatically within just one hour. Trainee paramedic Krystal Chapman live-tweeted a series of humorous photos showing herself progressively sinking into the growing crack in the asphalt on Pitt Road in North Curl Curl. Dressed in a coral top, blue trousers, and sunglasses, she began by cautiously placing her ankles into the hole. Within minutes, the pothole deepened enough to swallow her knees, then her waist. In her final image, she uses her hands to brace herself, preventing a full fall into the crevice. 'Sinkhole in North Curl Curl, Pitt Road!' she tweeted, tagging both the local newspaper, the Manly Daily, and Warringah Council. 'It’s getting worse by the minute!' she joked, as the situation escalated. Despite three orange cones marking the danger, she urged officials to act immediately. When Warringah Council responded asking for the location, she replied: '@warringah — it’s on Pitt Road in Curl Curl! Filled in overnight!' She later explained to the Manly Daily that the collapse was caused by a ruptured water pipe beneath the road.

article_content: On the Turkish side of the border, groups of men in T-shirts stand casually, smartphones raised, capturing the fiery explosions erupting just kilometers away in Kobane, Syria. Behind them, smoke billows from buildings targeted by U.S.-led airstrikes aimed at halting ISIS’s advance. But instead of fleeing or offering aid, these onlookers treat the destruction like a dramatic show — snapping photos as if at a festival. Kobane, a city of 400,000, lies so close to Turkey that its northern streets run parallel to the razor-wire fence separating the two nations. Mortars from ISIS have already struck homes in Turkish villages, yet Turkey’s military remains stationed nearby, watching — not intervening. The Kurdish defenders, outnumbered and undersupplied, hold on against armored ISIS units armed with weapons looted from Iraqi and Syrian army depots. Turkish officials refuse to support these fighters, labeling them as extensions of the PKK, a group President Erdogan has equated with ISIS itself. Meanwhile, Turkey’s prime minister demands a U.S.-imposed no-fly zone over Syria, insisting that without it, Turkey cannot bear the burden of refugees and cross-border attacks. Yet, critics point to troubling reports: Turkey reportedly allowed 180 detained ISIS fighters to rejoin their ranks in exchange for the release of 46 Turkish nationals captured in Mosul. The scene echoes eerie historical precedents — from 19th-century British tourists visiting Civil War battlefields to spectators lining hills near Quneitra in Israel’s Golan Heights, watching Syrian conflict unfold with sunglasses and picnic blankets. War, it seems, has become a grim form of entertainment for those safe enough to watch — and profitable enough to ignore.

article_content: Just days after Paul Ryan admitted he exaggerated his marathon time—claiming a sub-three-hour finish when he actually completed it in over four hours—his claims about mountain climbing are now under scrutiny. Ryan, Mitt Romney’s vice-presidential candidate, told a Wisconsin newspaper in 2009 that he had made 'close to 40 climbs' of Colorado’s 53 fourteeners—peaks over 14,000 feet. While the phrasing was vague, critics now argue that achieving such a number without living in Colorado would require an extraordinary commitment of time. Experts on SuperTopo, a climbing website, noted that completing 40 fourteeners without residing nearby would mean dedicating entire summers to climbing for over a decade—even for seasoned hikers, it’s a massive undertaking. Ryan’s campaign later clarified that 'close to 40' referred to total ascents, not unique peaks, and that he had been climbing for more than 20 years, often returning to the same mountains. The controversy follows Ryan’s admission that his 1990 Grandma’s Marathon time was 4 hours, 1 minute, and 25 seconds—not the 'two hour and fifty-something' he’d boasted to radio host Hugh Hewitt. His time places him behind Sarah Palin (3:59) and George W. Bush (3:44), but ahead of Al Gore (4:58). Critics contend that these embellishments reflect a broader pattern of manufactured authenticity to appeal to voters, particularly in swing states. They argue that such fabrications betray a disregard for truth and an assumption that the public won’t fact-check. Yet supporters point out that many athletes and outdoor enthusiasts accumulate climbs over decades without publicizing them—and that Ryan’s record may simply be misunderstood rather than invented.

article_content: Following the brutal killing of American journalist James Foley by ISIS, unsubstantiated claims emerged that a U.S. rescue mission failed due to delays in President Barack Obama’s approval. Retired military intelligence officer Tony Shaffer asserted on media platforms that the operation might have succeeded if authorized earlier—possibly in June—before the hostages were moved. He claimed Pentagon insiders believed intelligence grew stale due to prolonged deliberation, leading to the mission’s failure upon arrival. However, both the White House and the Department of Defense issued strong rebuttals, stating the mission was executed as soon as officials were confident it could succeed—and that the captives had already been relocated by the time U.S. forces arrived. The narrative, initially reported by The Sunday Times of London and widely shared online, triggered national debate. Meanwhile, Foley’s televised beheading, distributed by ISIS, horrified audiences globally. Some analysts now suspect the video was recorded months—or even more than a year—before its release, which would mean no rescue mission could have saved him regardless of timing. If confirmed, this would challenge the reliability of U.S. intelligence assessments during that period.

article_content: Rapper Young Jeezy, whose real name is Jay Wayne Jenkins, is facing serious criminal charges after allegedly assaulting his teenage son during a violent argument in September 2012. According to a police report, the incident began when the teen sent a text message to his father, triggering an explosive reaction. Jeezy reportedly entered the bathroom where his son was, slammed his head against the shower door, then picked him up and hurled him into a bedroom wall. When the boy attempted to flee downstairs, he was blocked by Jeezy’s bodyguard. The rapper then dragged him back inside, choked him, and threatened to kill him, saying, 'I’ll kill you' and 'I’ll put a bullet in your head right now.' The teen was further assaulted by being thrown against walls and kicked in the head. Two days after the incident, the boy returned to his mother, who noticed visible bruises and scratches and immediately contacted police. Jeezy turned himself in to authorities in Fulton County, Georgia, and was released on a $45,000 bond. He is scheduled to appear in an Atlanta court on January 29 to face felony charges of battery, terroristic threats, and false imprisonment. CNN’s Jane Caffrey contributed to this report.

article_content: New data reveals that the number of Britons out of work for more than a year has surged to 915,000 — the most in nearly two decades, last seen back in 1996. While overall unemployment dipped to 2.51 million, the lowest since last autumn, this improvement masks a deeper crisis: hundreds of thousands are stuck in prolonged joblessness, with over 460,000 having been without work for more than two years — the highest since 1997. Even as employment climbed to 29.7 million and Jobseeker’s Allowance claims fell to 1.478 million — their lowest point since March 2011 — many workers are struggling to survive. Wages rose just 1.7% over the past year, while inflation hit 2.9%, meaning real incomes are shrinking. Families are feeling the pinch like never before in over 100 years. The number of people not in the labor force also rose by 87,000 to 9.04 million, driven by more students, long-term sick individuals, and those retiring early. Youth unemployment improved slightly, dropping to 959,000, but still hovers at a troubling 20.9%. Unions have sounded alarms. Dave Prentis of Unison called long-term unemployment a 'personal tragedy,' stressing that even modest gains in job numbers offer little comfort to those enduring months or years without work. Frances O’Grady of the TUC warned that the labor market is far from healthy, with wages being eroded and young people still trapped in crisis conditions. Prime Minister David Cameron pointed to the drop in claimants and rise in employment as signs of progress, crediting government investments in apprenticeships — over a million started during this Parliament. Employment Minister Mark Hoban added that over half a million job vacancies exist, urging job seekers to take advantage of opportunities. But behind the statistics lie real lives: people whose skills fade, confidence wanes, and futures dim. For many, finding a job isn’t just about effort — it’s about access, support, and systemic change.

article_content: Inflation in the UK has dropped to its lowest level in five years, falling to 1.2% in September — well below the Bank of England’s 2% target. This sharp decline, driven by cheaper travel, electronics, dining, and food, means interest rate hikes may now be delayed until mid-2015. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) reported that the drop from 1.5% in August was steeper than expected. Food prices fell for the fifth consecutive month, marking the largest annual decline since 2002. Meanwhile, transport costs dropped 2.4% as airlines and ferry operators slashed prices after the summer season. Technology also played a major role: prices for laptops, tablets, printers, games consoles, and e-books all declined, contributing to the slowdown in inflation. Petrol and diesel prices also fell, by 0.8p and 0.7p per litre respectively, as global oil prices tumbled. Despite these gains, wage growth remains weak at just 0.7% annually — meaning most households are still seeing their incomes lag behind living costs. However, the government’s ‘triple lock’ policy ensures state pensions will rise by 2.5% next spring — or £2.85 per week — regardless of inflation levels. Chancellor George Osborne hailed the figures as a ‘double dose of good news’ for families and pensioners, standing on the steps of Number 11 Downing Street alongside Australia’s Treasurer Joe Hockey. His animated hand gestures drew comparisons to 1970s comedian Tommy Cooper, adding a light-hearted moment to the economic briefing. Meanwhile, housing prices continue to soar. The average UK home now costs £274,000, up 11.7% in a year. In London, the surge is even more dramatic: average property values hit £514,000 — a 19.6% jump. First-time buyers are struggling, with the average purchase price reaching £210,000 — up 12.9% year-on-year. Economists agree: with oil prices falling, currency strength reducing import costs, and supermarkets locked in price wars, inflation is unlikely to rise soon. Many now believe the Bank of England won’t raise rates until summer 2015 — if then. The pound weakened in response, reflecting reduced expectations for near-term monetary tightening. While the government and opposition praised the pension boost, Labour warned that low wage growth continues to hurt working families. As shadow treasury minister Catherine McKinnell noted: 'Total pay is rising at just 0.6% — half the rate of inflation.'

በላይ እየተቀነሰ ነው፣ ይህም ከ2002 በኋላ ታካናቸው ነው። ከዚያም የመንገድ እርምጃዎች 2.4% ተቀነሰዋል፣ ምክንያቱም የአየር ማንኛውም እና የባህር ድርጅቶች በዓመት የታህደው ዘመን በኋላ የእርምጃ ድርጅቶችን አቀናበሩ። ተክኖሎጂም በተለይ የተሳሳተ አስተዋጽኦ ነበረው፡ የሌፕቶፕ፣ ቻርጄር፣ ማተሚያ እና የኮምፒዩተር article_content: Barcelona is preparing to officially welcome Luis Suarez as their newest signing, pending resolution of his four-month global suspension imposed by FIFA after he bit Italy’s Giorgio Chiellini during the 2014 World Cup. While the announcement was initially slated for Thursday, officials are waiting for clarity on the suspension’s scope before proceeding — possibly pushing the formal reveal to Friday. The move becomes financially viable thanks to the impending departure of Alexis Sanchez, who has agreed to join Arsenal for a fee of £30 million. Sanchez, a Chilean international, chose the Gunners over strong bids from Liverpool and Juventus. His representatives are currently in London finalizing personal terms, including a weekly salary reportedly matching that of Mesut Özil — approximately £140,000. With Sanchez’s transfer nearing completion, Barcelona can now proceed with its £75 million offer for Suarez, who scored prolifically for Liverpool before his controversial exit. Fan enthusiasm is palpable: merchandise retailers have already begun selling 'Suarez 9' jerseys ahead of his debut. Meanwhile, Arsenal continues strengthening its squad. A £11 million deal for Newcastle right-back Mathieu Debuchy is nearly finalized following his medical, and he will step into the role vacated by Bacary Sagna, who has moved to Manchester City. Talks with QPR striker Loic Remy, valued at £8 million, are ongoing, though disagreements over wages — Remy earns £75,000 per week at QPR — remain unresolved. article_content: Matthew Hayes, 12, died after being hit by a bus on Friday afternoon near a busy supermarket on Ryhope Street South in Sunderland. His sister, Rehanna, left a heartfelt note at the roadside in memory of her 'baby brother.' 'Words can't describe how much I'm missing you,' she wrote. 'I shouldn't be writing this — it shouldn't be like this. My baby brother, just 12 years old — it doesn't seem real.' In her letter, Rehanna recalled their life together in Moorside, Wyatt, Sunderland — playing video games, wrestling, watching TV, and chasing each other with Nerf guns. 'I'm physically heartbroken,' she wrote. 'I'm trying to stay strong for Mum and Dad, but I just can't accept that you're gone.' 'I'm glad I gave you a hug and a kiss before you left for school on Friday. I could have been a better sister — and for that, I am so, so sorry. I honestly love you more than anything in the world.' Rehanna remembered how, on Christmas Eve 2000 — the day Matthew was born — her family let her choose his name. 'I just need you to come and tell me everything's alright... but it's not. I can't believe this has happened.' Matthew’s family also released a statement through Northumbria Police, thanking everyone who tried to save him: 'We want to thank all the people who tried to save Matthew’s life on Friday — including his school friends, members of the public, and emergency services. We know everyone did their very best.' 'We know you’ll always be with us. I remember when we used to fight over who got to hold you. This shouldn’t be like this. RIP, baby. Sleep tight. We’ll see you soon. I love you so much — words cannot describe it.'
translated_content: ማቴው ሁይስ, 12, በየومዕድ እና በሩይሆ መንገድ ላይ በአንድ ባስ ላይ ተደርጎ ሞተ። እያሱ ራሄና, በመቃብር ስፍራ ላይ ለ'ወለድ አخዬ' ቀልድ አቀረበታል። 'የቃላት አይቻልም ስለምን እንደሚያስፈልግኝ ፡፡ እኔ እዚህ እንዳጽፋ አይኖርም፣ እዚህ እንደዚህ አይኖርም፣ 12 ዓመት የሆነ ወለድ አخዬ — እዚህ እውነት አይደለም።' በየት እንደተቀመጠ ማቴው በሞርሲድ እና በዊያት ክፍል ውስጥ እንደ የተጠቀሙ አገልግሎቶች፦ የኮምፒዩተር ጊዜ ማግኘት፣ የመጠን መጠን ማድረግ፣ የቲቪ ማየት እና ነርፍ ጣቢያዎችን በቤት ውስጥ መጠራጠር አስታየቷል። 'እኔ በፊزيካዊ ሁኔታ ስሜት አለሁ፣' ራሄና አሳለቷል። 'እኔ ለአሜ እና ለአባት ለመቆየት እናደርጋለሁ፣ ነገር ግን እኔ እንደምትወሰድ አይችልም።' 'በየዓመቱ ለማቴው ለመሄድ በፊት እኔ እንደ አቀረበኩ እና እንደ አቅርበኩ እናነኛለሁ፣ እኔ ለሚያስፈልገው የአንደኛ አክሮ ሆን ሊሆን እንደሚችል አይደለም፣ እና ለዚህ እናነኛለሁ በጣም በጣም። እኔ በዓለም ውስጥ ለምንም አይደለም እንደሚያወቅህ እንደሚያስደስትኝ ነው።' ራሄና እንደ ማቴው በ2000 ዓ.ም. ክርስምስ ማንቃቂ ቀን ለመውለድ እና እኔ እንደ ስም ምርጫ እንደተጠየቀ አስታየቷል። 'እኔ ብቻ ለማቴው ለመመለስ እና ለማን ስለ ሁሉ በደለ እንዲያመለክት እንደሚፈልግኝ ነው… ነገር ግን እና አይደለም። እኔ እዚህ ስለ ሆነ እንደሚያምነው አይችልም።' ማቴው የወላደቱ አገልግሎት በኖርትምቢሪያ ፕለስ አስተያየት አቅርቦታቸው ላይ በየዓመቱ ለሚያስደስተው ሁሉ እንዲህ አሳለቷል፦ 'በየዓመቱ ለማቴው ለመጠጥ የሞከሩ ሁሉንም አመሰግናለን — ለማቴው የተማረጉ የትምህርት ቤት ሰዎች፣ ለአጠቃላይ ሰዎች እና ለእጅጉ አገልግሎቶች። እኛ እናውቃለን ሁሉም እንደ ስለ ሆነ እንደ አደረገው ነው።' 'እኛ እናውቃለን እርስዎ በድምር ውስጥ እንደሚሆን ነው። እኔ ስለ እንደ ስለ ለመግዛት ስለ ሆነ እንደ ስለ ሆነ እንደ ሆነ ነው። እዚህ እንደዚህ አይኖርም። አር.ኢ.ፒ. ወለድ። በደለ ይናሙኑ። እኛ በደለ ይናሙኑ። እኔ በጣም እወቅህ ፣ ቃላት አይቻሉ ለመግለጽ።'

article_content: Jack Roberts, a highly respected ice climber with over four decades of experience, tragically lost his life on Sunday after suffering a heart attack during a climb at Bridal Veil Ice Falls in Colorado. The 58-year-old veteran fell approximately 60 feet from the 365-foot frozen cascade near Telluride around 12:20 p.m. Though his climbing partner stabilized him after the fall and he remained conscious for about an hour, Roberts succumbed to cardiac arrest before emergency responders could reach him. The remote location, accessible only via snowmobile after navigating a steep, icy canyon, delayed rescue efforts. Eighteen first responders spent nearly 40 minutes attempting CPR, but were unable to revive him. Known for his deep passion for the sport, Roberts authored the acclaimed 2005 book 'Colorado Ice' and contributed extensively to climbing publications. In a 2021 YouTube video, he described ice climbing as an intimate, transformative experience — one that offered climbers a rare connection to nature unlike rock climbing. He lived in Boulder and was survived by his wife, who was abroad when she received the devastating news.

article_content: A teaching assistant in Blackpool slipped on a jigsaw puzzle piece, sustaining a fractured coccyx and chronic back pain. The incident led to nearly £40,000 in payouts from the local council—£4,800 in direct compensation to the assistant and £32,000 in legal fees. This case was one of 281 workplace injury claims made by teachers and teaching assistants across England last year. Collectively, these claims cost local authorities £7 million in taxpayer funds. Analysis reveals that for every £1 paid in compensation, another £1 went to legal representatives, many operating on controversial 'no-win no-fee' agreements. Among the most significant payouts: £114,000 to a Birmingham teacher who developed a stress disorder after intervening in a student fight; £32,000 to a teacher who slipped on ice; £25,000 for injuries caused by falling storage cupboard items; and £4,500 and £16,000 for two teachers struck by falling projectors. Other incidents included: a Harrow Council payout of £24,000 after a student collided with a teacher on a scooter; £2,500 in West Sussex for vocal cord damage from chemical fumes; £1,500 for recurring headaches triggered by a faulty cupboard door; £7,500 for a slip on a manhole cover in Croydon; and £9,000 for a crushed hand while moving furniture. In Plymouth, a teacher received £19,000 in compensation after injuring their arm breaking up a student brawl—with an additional £26,000 paid to their solicitor and £8,000 in the council’s own legal expenses, bringing the total to £53,000. In Rotherham, £4,750 was paid after a faulty handrail gave way during a fall, and £2,000 for slipping on food left on the floor. In Bromley, a teacher received £10,000 after tripping over an extension cord in a poorly lit classroom. Critics, including the TaxPayers' Alliance and the Campaign for Real Education, warn that a growing 'compensation culture' is draining education budgets. They argue that excessive claims and fear of litigation are forcing schools to eliminate outdoor activities, field trips, and even physical play—all under the guise of safety. Andy Silvester of the TaxPayers' Alliance stated: 'Either schools aren’t safe, or they’re paying out too easily on dubious claims. Every pound spent on compensation is a pound taken from classrooms.' Christopher McGowan of the Campaign for Real Education added: 'Health and safety rules are no longer protecting children—they're robbing them of childhood. What was once a system for serious injuries has become a compensation free-for-all.'

article_content: Waris Grant, a 37-year-old arts and music teacher at Public School 256 in Brooklyn, has been arrested after allegedly paying a 16-year-old boy for oral sex — an act prosecutors classify as promoting prostitution under New York law. The teenager, who attends a different public school, disclosed the encounter to his parents, who alerted police. Grant was taken into custody on Thursday and reportedly admitted to the behavior during questioning. Although he has been reassigned to a non-classroom role by the New York City Department of Education, he continues to receive his annual salary of $72,990. Grant, who has worked at P.S. 256 for over four years and lost his long-term partner, Jamall King, several years ago, now faces charges of promoting prostitution, engaging in a criminal sex act, and acting in a manner injurious to a child. His bail has been set at $7,500. The incident occurred at an unknown time and place, and the minor’s identity remains legally protected. P.S. 256, located on Kosciuszko Street and led by Principal Sharyn Hemphill, serves more than 350 students from Pre-K through sixth grade. How Grant came to know the boy remains unclear.

article_content: Tooele, Utah (CNN) — Syria has been granted a year to destroy its chemical weapons arsenal or risk a U.S. military strike. But few realize the United States — along with Russia — has yet to fully eliminate its own vast stockpiles of deadly nerve agents. Both nations signed the 1990s Chemical Weapons Convention, which bans the development, production, and storage of chemical weapons. Yet both missed the 2012 deadline set by the treaty — a fact underscored when the 2013 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), the body overseeing Syria’s disarmament. The Nobel Committee explicitly noted: 'Certain states have not observed the deadline... This applies especially to the USA and Russia.' The U.S. estimates it will take at least another decade to destroy the remaining 10% of its arsenal — over 3,100 tons — stored at two sites: Pueblo, Colorado, and Bluegrass, Kentucky. Russia, according to the OPCW, has more than five times that amount left. Syria’s stockpile is estimated at roughly 1,000 tons, scattered across dozens of locations. The U.N. has set a mid-2014 deadline for its destruction, with inspectors cautiously optimistic despite operating in active war zones. Yet experts like Wade Mathews, who once led U.S. chemical demilitarization efforts, question whether Syria can succeed. 'We spent billions, coordinated multiple government agencies, and operated in a secure environment,' Mathews said. 'Those conditions simply don’t exist in Syria.' Mathews worked at the Tooele Army Depot in Utah — once home to 43% of America’s chemical weapons. The facility stored mustard gas and nerve agents since World War II. After 16 years of painstaking, zero-casualty destruction, the last munition was neutralized in March 2023. Today, the U.S. continues its work in Pueblo, where 2,600 tons of liquid mustard gas will be destroyed starting in 2015 — a process expected to conclude in 2019. In Kentucky, 523 tons of VX, sarin, and mustard agent will be tackled from 2020 to 2023. Syria’s challenge is starkly different. The U.S. Department of Defense warns against comparing its domestic, well-resourced program to the chaotic, international effort in Syria. Even if Syria cooperates, finding, securing, and safely destroying weapons amid civil war remains unprecedented. While Syria denies using chemical weapons — blaming rebels instead — the August 2013 Damascus attack, which killed over 1,400 people, triggered global action. Now, the world watches to see if diplomacy can achieve what war could not.

article_content: A popular Manhattan restaurant frequently visited by celebrities is under investigation by the Department of Health after a pregnant woman contracted a foodborne illness following a meal there, according to published reports. Freeman's Restaurant, a trendy Lower East Side dining spot described as a 'hunting lodge-inspired brunch destination,' is being investigated for a norovirus outbreak that causes vomiting and diarrhea, a Department of Health spokesperson told the New York Post. The restaurant currently holds an 'A' rating — the highest possible score for compliance with city health codes. Health officials requested stool samples from employees to rule out viral transmission, but Freeman's stated that tests confirmed no presence of the virus among staff. 'The Department of Health investigated Freeman's, concluded its findings, and found no link or transmission of the virus at the restaurant,' said restaurant spokesman Eden Grimaldi to the Post. Norovirus is transmitted through fecal contamination and person-to-person contact, infecting approximately 20 million people annually. 'They came and checked everything yesterday… tested everyone… took stool samples,' a staff member told the Post. The restaurant is a favorite among celebrities such as Mary Kate and Ashley Olsen, who live or spend time in lower Manhattan. Loyal patrons quickly defended the restaurant, noting that an investigation does not equate to proven wrongdoing. Freeman's remains open with its 'A' rating intact, according to Grimaldi.

article_content: Harry Kane, an English striker driven by an insatiable hunger for goals and an even greater passion for hard work, may not be Tottenham’s most technically polished player—but he is unquestionably shining brightest right now. On Sunday, he netted his 11th goal of the season, powering home a decisive header in Tottenham’s 2-1 away victory over Swansea. It marked his third match-winning goal in a 2-1 away win this campaign—points that could mean the difference between finishing seventh and eleventh in the Premier League. At the Liberty Stadium, Kane covered a staggering 13.1 kilometers—tied for the most among visiting players, alongside Christian Eriksen. His relentless energy and instinctive finishing have turned him into a fan favorite at White Hart Lane. Born in Chingford and raised as a Spurs supporter, Kane embodies the club’s grassroots spirit: 'Harry Kane—he’s one of our own.' Aged just 21, Kane began the season as the understudy to Emmanuel Adebayor. Today, he defines the opposite end of the spectrum: where Adebayor was criticized for lack of effort, Kane gives everything. His 17 goals from 23 Premier League starts speak volumes—and his influence extends beyond scoring. In last month’s 2-1 win over Everton, though he didn’t find the net, his two assists earned praise from pundit Jamie Carragher, who called him the best player on the pitch. Kane’s journey has been anything but conventional. He climbed from League One with Leyton Orient, through Millwall, Norwich, and Leicester, earning eight goals in the Europa League along the way. No flashy transfer fee, no inflated reputation—just relentless determination. In an era where young talents often demand instant promotion, Kane earned his place the hard way. Though some question his finesse compared to elite forwards, Kane trades in results—and he’s cash-rich. His ability to sense danger and finish with composure is rare. And he never shies away when chances go astray. With his drive and authenticity, he’s not just a striker—he’s a symbol of belief for Spurs fans. And with his sights set on the England senior team—despite eligibility for the Republic of Ireland—Kane has made it clear: when he sets a target, he hits it. Roy Hodgson would do well to take notice.

article_content: After nearly two decades on the run, Eddie Maher — famously known as 'Fast Eddie' — was arrested in Missouri in early 2012, ending a 19-year escape following one of Britain’s most notorious armored van robberies. In March 2013, he was sentenced to five years in prison at Southwark Crown Court for stealing £1.2 million from a Securicor vehicle outside a Lloyds Bank in Suffolk in January 1993. His capture came not from international manhunt efforts, but from someone close to him: his daughter-in-law, Jessica King. She reached out to U.S. federal agents after discovering Maher’s true identity through an online search. King told ITV’s Daybreak she acted out of fear for her safety, not the £100,000 reward offered by Securicor. 'He threatened me when he found out I knew,' she said. 'It wasn’t about money — it was about survival.' Maher had built a new life under the alias 'Stephen King', using forged documents and purchasing homes in Colorado and New Hampshire with cash from the heist. Despite living lavishly for years, he eventually became destitute. Meanwhile, his pension from his former job as a London firefighter — frozen since his disappearance — had grown to approximately £125,000 due to annual inflation adjustments. UK police now aim to reclaim that pension fund under the Criminal Justice Act, arguing the money was earned through lawful employment but should not benefit someone who fled justice after committing a major crime. Maher, who declared bankruptcy in the U.S., claims all stolen funds are long gone. His legal team and prosecutors will debate the matter in upcoming hearings at Ipswich Crown Court. Interestingly, King’s path to marrying Maher’s son, Lee, was unconventional — she left her previous partner after Lee won the lottery. When their money ran out, she googled the Maher name and stumbled upon the decades-old wanted notice. She had no idea the reward was legitimate until after she contacted authorities. Still, she expressed no regret. 'It was the right thing to do,' she said. 'And if the money comes, it would help me raise my child alone.'
