article_content: In Steubenville, Ohio, two 16-year-old members of the local high school’s football team, Ma'lik Richmond and Trenton Mays, face serious criminal charges related to the alleged sexual assault of a classmate last August. As their juvenile trial approaches in February, their defense lawyers are sounding alarms: widespread online exposure of images and videos tied to the case — leaked by the activist group Anonymous — may have already damaged their chances of receiving a fair hearing. One widely circulated photo shows the two teens carrying what appears to be an unresponsive young woman; a separate video features other youths laughing as they recount the incident. Richmond’s attorney, Walter Madison, clarified on CNN that while his client is visible in the photo, he is not in the video — and emphasized that the girl depicted was not unconscious, contrary to many reports. Madison warned that the viral spread of this material has effectively turned the case into a public spectacle, threatening constitutional rights. Mays’ lawyer, Adam Nemann, echoed these fears, noting that witnesses may now be too afraid to testify, fearing backlash or social stigma, and might invoke their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination. Complicating matters further, local prosecutors and police had close relationships with Steubenville High, prompting Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine to step in. DeWine acknowledged the commonality of such conflicts in tight-knit communities but stressed that the real harm lies in the digital retraumatization of the victim. 'Every time a new post goes up,' he said, 'she suffers all over again.' He condemned Anonymous’ campaign of public shaming, arguing that while outrage is understandable, justice must be decided in courtrooms — not comment sections.

article_content: Unknown gunmen opened fire on a crowd outside Ricardo Flores Magon Elementary School in Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, on Wednesday afternoon, killing one person and injuring four others, according to municipal police spokesman Adrían Sánchez. Sánchez said the attackers were pursuing a man who had fled with a woman toward the school. They caught up to them near the campus and fired indiscriminately into the crowd, disregarding the presence of bystanders. School was in session at 2 p.m. local time (3 p.m. ET), with students aged 10 to 11 in their first week of classes. None of the children were physically harmed, Sánchez confirmed. However, journalists on site reported that children witnessed the shooting. Teachers, still in shock, declined to speak with reporters. Among the injured were three women and one man — including the woman accompanying the targeted individual. All three women were waiting outside the school to pick up their children. Authorities found no indication that any victims were involved in drug trafficking, though the possibility remains under investigation. Witnesses told CNN the suspects fled in a Volkswagen Jetta armed with AK-47 rifles — weapons commonly associated with Mexican drug cartels. Earlier this week, the Chihuahua state government reported that 225 women had been killed in Ciudad Juárez this year. Located across the border from El Paso, Texas, Ciudad Juárez has long been a focal point of Mexico’s most severe drug-related violence. CNN stringer Arturo Chacón contributed to this report.

article_content: A new book, 'The Good Son: JFK Jr. and the Mother He Loved' by Christopher Andersen, claims that John F. Kennedy Jr. had a brief romantic relationship with Madonna in 1988, shortly after her separation from Sean Penn. According to the book, Madonna reportedly pursued JFK Jr., telling friends she believed the connection would be 'cosmic'. Friends of Madonna, including dancer Erika Belle, say JFK Jr. was immediately captivated by her. The pair reportedly met regularly at a health club where they shared a personal trainer and sometimes jogged together in Central Park early in the morning. Despite keeping their relationship private from the press, JFK Jr. introduced Madonna to his mother, Jackie Onassis, at her Central Park apartment. At the time, Madonna was still legally married to Penn, and she signed the guestbook as 'Mrs. Sean Penn'. Jackie Onassis reportedly disapproved of Madonna for multiple reasons: her use of religious imagery, which the Vatican had criticized, and especially her appearance on the cover of Vanity Fair in 1991 dressed as Marilyn Monroe—a figure associated with her husband President John F. Kennedy’s past infidelities. Andersen recounts an anecdote in which JFK Jr., staying at Billy Noonan’s home in Hyannis Port, played a voicemail from Madonna in Rome: 'I’m drunk and when I see you next I’m going to take your...' The message ended in explicit language. Noonan, stunned, asked if it was really Madonna. JFK Jr. replied matter-of-factly, 'She’s a sexual dynamo.' Meanwhile, JFK Jr. was still in a committed relationship with Christina Haag—whom Jackie Onassis hoped he would marry. The affair with Madonna remained hidden from her. Sean Penn allegedly confronted JFK Jr. at a tribute party for Robert De Niro at Tribeca Grill, saying, 'I know who you are. You owe me an apology.' JFK Jr. reportedly left quickly, aware of Penn’s volatile reputation. JFK Jr. was also linked to actress Sarah Jessica Parker during this era. He died in a plane crash in 1999 alongside his wife, Carolyn Bessette, and her sister, Lauren.

article_content: After Thanksgiving, many families are left with mountains of uneaten turkey — but what if those leftovers could become something even better? Instead of letting perfectly good food go to waste, top chefs across the U.S. are turning yesterday’s meal into tomorrow’s masterpiece. The USDA estimates that about 35% of turkey meat is eaten only after the holiday, while the EPA reports that over 100 million tons of food ends up in landfills every year, nearly two-thirds of it from homes and restaurants. With that in mind, we asked professional chefs to share their most clever, delicious ways to reuse holiday scraps — and the results are mouthwatering. At Ritz-Carlton Sarasota, Chef Andrew Thompson brines his turkey for a full day in herbs, garlic, and brown sugar, then cooks it low and slow using sous vide to lock in moisture. His go-to leftover hack? A cold sandwich piled high with cranberry sauce — simple, but unforgettable. He even suggests spicing up the bird with curry powder beforehand for a bold twist. Meanwhile, in Albany, Dylon Ruiz transforms turkey and mashed potatoes into Latin-inspired papas rellenas: spiced turkey stew wrapped in a potato-stuffing dough, then fried until golden. It’s comfort food with a global flair. Nik Fields, known as The Chic Chef, turns mashed potatoes into crispy croquettes using stuffing as a binder, makes sweet potato hash with peppers and onions, and even bakes cranberry sauce into fluffy pancakes. Her motto: 'Nothing goes to waste — everything gets reinvented.' Chef Dan Vargo flips the script on chicken and waffles by using leftover stuffing and mashed potatoes to form crispy waffles, topping them with lightly fried turkey bits and a spicy cranberry relish made with lime, maple, and jalapeño. Marco Grajeda keeps it classic but elevated: toasted potato rolls, warm turkey, melted Muenster, and a side of gravy for dipping. Simple, satisfying, and surprisingly elegant. Craig Tooker stuffs empanadas with turkey, sweet potatoes, stuffing, and gravy — then serves them with a drizzle of cranberry sauce. Perfect for snacking or sharing. Coatiest Gabbidon from the Ritz-Carlton St. Thomas encourages thinking outside the box: try smoked turkey wings glazed with cranberry, or puff pastry tapas filled with turkey. He even recommends smoking turkey with pimento berries or brewing it with Red Stripe beer for unexpected depth. And finally, Chef Gavin Lambert reimagines Thanksgiving as ramen night: simmering turkey bones with veggie scraps overnight, thickening the broth with gravy and cranberry sauce, then serving it over instant noodles with roasted Brussels sprouts and candied yams. He even saves the stock for future soups — because why waste a drop?

article_content: Jack Wilshere returned to peak form in Arsenal’s thrilling 2-2 draw with Manchester City, silencing critics and reminding everyone why he’s so special. Playing with joy and composure, he controlled the game from the opposition half, capped by a perfectly executed chip past Joe Hart. While Roy Hodgson sees him as a holding midfielder, his brilliance shines brightest in advanced roles — and England would benefit greatly if he played there regularly. Diego Costa has announced himself in the Premier League with astonishing force: seven goals in four games — faster than any Chelsea striker in recent memory. He’s scoring with both feet and his head, thriving alongside Cesc Fabregas, and seems to be terrifying defenders. Comparisons to Didier Drogba are no longer speculative — Costa may well be the real successor. Aston Villa pulled off a stunning 1-0 win at Anfield, shutting down Liverpool’s attack with disciplined defending. By isolating Gerrard, Coutinho, and Henderson, and letting the center-backs have the ball, Paul Lambert’s side exposed Liverpool’s lack of cutting edge without Suarez or Sturridge. Philippe Senderos dominated Mario Balotelli, and Gabriel Agbonlahor’s goal sealed a tactically brilliant victory. Manchester United finally secured their first win under Louis van Gaal, dismantling QPR 4-0 with a dynamic diamond midfield. Angel di Maria dazzled, but Ander Herrera’s energy, vision, and goal-scoring instinct stole the show. While a back three may be coming, this formation looked sharp — and deserves to stay. John Stones delivered another commanding performance in Everton’s 2-0 win at West Brom. With Sylvain Distin injured, the 20-year-old showed maturity beyond his years: excellent positioning, recovery pace, and comfort on the ball. He’s not just filling in — he’s ready to lead the defense. Southampton defied expectations with a 4-0 thrashing of Newcastle. Graziano Pelle, signed as a replacement for Rickie Lambert, has already forged a potent partnership with Dusan Tadic. His technical ability as a tall striker is rare, and his two goals underscore Southampton’s surprising strength. Leicester City extended their incredible scoring run to 34 consecutive league games, with Leonardo Ulloa netting the winner against Stoke. His composure under pressure and knack for finishing from tight angles make him a revelation. With Esteban Cambiasso adding experience, Leicester are quietly becoming title contenders. Aaron Ramsey remains Arsenal’s engine: directly involved in seven goals in his last eight league appearances. Since last season, no Gunner has provided more assists — nine in total. Newcastle’s plight worsens: just five points from their last 36, and fan protests demanding Alan Pardew’s exit grow louder. Meanwhile, West Brom’s home form is a disaster — only one win in 11 league games at The Hawthorns. In other stats: Morgan Schneiderlin has already matched his entire last season’s goal tally in just three games for Southampton. Harry Kane’s own goal was the 100th of the Premier League season.

article_content: Former Pakistani cricketer Abdul Razzaq has reignited controversy with remarks about India’s defeat in the ODI World Cup final against Australia on November 19, 2023. In a viral social media clip, Razzaq stated, 'Cricket won and India lost. Had India won, it would have been a very sad moment for the game.' He criticized the pitch conditions in the final, calling them the worst he’d ever seen in an ICC final, and claimed India exploited uneven playing conditions — citing high scores in one semifinal (India 400/5 vs. South Africa) and lower scores in the other (Australia 350/8 vs. England), followed by Australia’s 270/7 and India’s 240 in the final. 'There should be fair pitches and a balanced atmosphere for both teams,' he added. Razzaq also suggested that if Virat Kohli had scored a century, India might have won. These comments follow a history of inflammatory statements by Pakistani cricketers toward India. In the past, Hasan Raza accused the ICC and BCCI of providing special balls to aid Indian pacers; Inzamam-ul-Haq falsely claimed Harbhajan Singh considered converting to Islam — a claim Harbhajan firmly denied. Razzaq himself previously drew backlash for derogatory remarks about actress Aishwarya Rai, later apologizing. His latest remarks have once again stirred tensions between the two cricketing giants.

article_content: Daniel Domscheit-Berg, a prominent spokesperson for WikiLeaks, has announced his departure from the organization, citing deep structural flaws and irreconcilable differences with founder Julian Assange. According to Germany’s Der Spiegel, Domscheit-Berg — who previously operated under the alias Daniel Schmitt — said the group’s explosive growth following the release of 76,000 U.S. military documents on the Afghanistan war left it ill-equipped to manage its operations effectively. 'Under the immense pressure after the document releases, we failed to restructure properly,' Domscheit-Berg explained. 'This has led to critical errors piling up — and I can no longer bear responsibility for them.' Unlike most public faces of WikiLeaks, who are typically Assange himself, Domscheit-Berg was one of few authorized representatives. He claimed his disagreements with Assange centered on the founder’s growing consolidation of power and reluctance to reduce his public profile amid serious sexual assault allegations in Sweden last month. 'I believed Assange should have stepped back quietly to address those issues while continuing his work out of the spotlight,' Domscheit-Berg told Der Spiegel. 'But he interpreted my suggestion as a personal attack.' The spokesperson also accused Assange of unilaterally suspending him a month ago — acting as prosecutor, judge, and executioner in one person. 'Every criticism was met with accusations of disloyalty,' he said. Despite his exit, Domscheit-Berg confirmed WikiLeaks continues to hold a substantial backlog of documents — including 15,000 more on the Afghanistan war — that urgently require processing and publication.

article_content: Multi-millionaire lottery winners Charles and Penelope Gillion have chosen to stay in their modest, red-brick, semi-detached council home in Corby—despite winning £38 million in the Euromillions earlier this year. Charlie, 64, is one of 12 bus drivers in Corby who shared the jackpot, while Penelope, 65, is a retired cleaner. Rather than splurging on luxury homes or vacations, the couple has opted to maintain their quiet, familiar life. They are currently waiting for Corby Borough Council to complete the valuation process so they can officially purchase their home of 30 years. With many other tenants also seeking to buy their homes, the process has taken nearly ten weeks—and they’ve yet to receive a visit from a valuer. The Gillions have not taken a holiday, upgraded their car, or changed their routines. They still shop at Asda, walk to local stores, and remain deeply connected to family and neighbors. Penelope, originally from Scotland, says: 'We’re still here. We haven’t moved on. We’re just waiting. We’re not looking for flash cars or mansions—we’re happy as we are.' The couple intends to eventually give their home to their granddaughter and her young son. With three children, ten grandchildren, and six great-grandchildren nearby, they have no intention of leaving Corby. Neighbors describe them as kind, genuine, and unchanged. Margaret Donnachie, a longtime neighbor, said: 'They’re just lovely people. No airs, no graces. I’m happy for them.' A former syndicate member, Hazel Loveday, 36, had left the group shortly before the win.

article_content: David Lancos, 59, of Pennsylvania, convinced a woman he was dying of cancer to obtain $15,000 to fund his gambling addiction, police say. He met Judith Brown, also 59, while watching harness racing — a form of horse racing — at a casino and racetrack in Butler County. Lancos told Brown he had cancer and could not afford treatment. Moved by compassion, she began paying him $300 per month in December 2012, continuing until March 2014. He also requested an undisclosed sum for two trips to a cancer center in Philadelphia and demanded $9,000 to pay legal fees, claiming he could no longer work and had to sell his share of the family business. Brown borrowed $9,000 from a bank after Lancos promised to repay her — but never received repayment. She later discovered he did not have cancer and contacted police. By then, she had lost $14,790. When officers attempted to arrest Lancos, they found he was already jailed on unrelated charges. During questioning, Lancos admitted he had spent all the money gambling. He has been charged with theft by deception and is being held on $10,000 bail.

article_content: Legendary comic creators Matt Wagner (Grendel) and Kelley Jones (Batman: Knightfall) have announced a bold new collaboration: a graphic novel prequel to Bram Stoker’s Dracula, titled DRACULA—BOOK 1: THE IMPALER. Rather than retelling the classic tale, the story delves into the formative years of Vlad III — the 15th-century Voivode of Wallachia — as he seeks dark powers to survive the relentless advance of the Ottoman Empire. His descent into monstrosity unfolds within the shadowy halls of the Scholomance, a legendary academy of forbidden arts. Writer Matt Wagner describes the project as a labor of love, born from decades of fascination with Dracula’s enigmatic origins. 'Our version is bloody, sexy, and monstrous — deeply rooted in Stoker’s vision, but not a retelling. This is the hidden history behind the myth,' he says. Artist Kelley Jones brings his signature gothic, atmospheric style — evoking the moody aesthetics of 90s Vertigo Comics — to render Dracula’s harrowing transformation. The visuals promise chilling detail and visceral horror. Though both creators previously contributed to Sandman: Seasons of Mist, this marks their first direct partnership. The project is now live on Kickstarter, featuring exclusive concept art and early previews. For fans of mythic horror and psychological depth, DRACULA—BOOK 1: THE IMPALER offers not just a comic — but a dark origin story waiting to be unearthed.

article_content: This past weekend, Disney’s animated hit Big Hero 6 soared past Christopher Nolan’s space epic Interstellar at the box office, defying predictions of a tight race. The heartwarming tale of a young genius and his lovable, puffy robot earned an estimated $56.2 million — a strong start fueled by Disney’s savvy marketing, tying it to the massive success of Frozen and Wreck-It Ralph. Meanwhile, Interstellar, starring Matthew McConaughey as a pilot searching for a new home for humanity amid Earth’s collapse, pulled in around $50 million. But experts warn that number could dip even lower once final figures are confirmed. Interestingly, this marks only the fourth time two films have launched with over $50 million in the same weekend — and every prior instance saw animation triumph over live action: WALL-E beat Wanted in 2008, Madagascar 3 topped Prometheus in 2012, and Monsters University outpaced World War Z in 2013. Analysts are digging into the numbers: Did Interstellar’s longer runtime limit showtimes? Did Disney’s 3D premiums outperform IMAX surcharges? And with Big Hero 6 playing in 200 more theaters yet averaging nearly $1,000 per venue, it’s clear audiences simply preferred the cartoon. Elsewhere, Gone Girl kept its momentum, landing in the top five for its sixth weekend and inching toward $150 million domestically. In limited release, The Theory of Everything — featuring Eddie Redmayne’s Oscar-bait portrayal of Stephen Hawking — exploded with $206,000 from just five theaters, a stellar per-screen average. With few new contenders next week, Big Hero 6 and Interstellar will battle again for the top spot — until The Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 1 arrives on November 21 to sweep everything aside.

article_content: Early Sunday morning, 18-year-old Naomi McClendon, a first-year student at Arizona State University, tragically fell from a seventh-floor balcony at an off-campus apartment in Tempe, Arizona. According to police, surveillance video shows her alone on the railing, appearing heavily intoxicated. She was not pushed or assisted by anyone — authorities confirm foul play is not suspected. Sgt. Mike Pooley of the Tempe Police Department described how she appeared to straddle the railing, then slipped, desperately trying to grab hold before plummeting. Friends were inside the apartment at the time. Witnesses outside the building recalled hearing a loud thud and seeing her lying motionless on the ground. McClendon had attended a party the previous night, and police are now investigating how she obtained alcohol despite being underage. A toxicology report is pending to check for additional substances in her system. Her boyfriend, Noah Schmidt, posted an emotional message on Facebook, lashing out in grief: 'You took away the most amazing person you ever created. F**k you God.' He later followed up with 'love you so much,' accompanied by photos of her. Hundreds of friends and strangers responded with messages of sympathy. McClendon, a talented keyboardist in a local band, had only recently moved away from home to begin college. The apartment complex has been shaken by the loss, with residents recalling the moment the news spread.

article_content: In December 2012, 26-year-old fashion designer Shaun Akanbi was found dead in his shared flat in Kilburn, north London, after being stabbed five times. His body was discovered following concerns from family and police that he hadn't been seen for three days. Akanbi, who launched the streetwear label Billy Boyce while studying at the London College of Fashion in 2009, had dressed high-profile artists including Ms. Dynamite and Tinie Tempah, making him a respected figure in the UK fashion scene. Achraf Jandara, then 20, is charged with murder. Prosecutors say Jandara met Akanbi through Facebook, possibly with romantic or sexual intentions, and used that connection to gain entry to the flat. Once inside, he allegedly attacked Akanbi, stole valuables—including clothing from the Billy Boyce collection—and fled the scene. CCTV footage captured Jandara leaving the building carrying a rucksack and trolley bag, both filled with stolen goods and wearing a jacket bearing Akanbi’s brand logo. Forensic evidence linked Jandara directly to the crime scene: his DNA was found on a coffee mug in Akanbi’s bedroom, and his footprint was discovered on the floor. Investigators also confirmed that Jandara’s cousin later sold Akanbi’s MacBook for £160. Despite this, Jandara insists he was innocent, claiming he stumbled upon the body and didn’t know what to do—yet he took multiple items from the flat before leaving. Prosecutor Peter Finnigan QC challenged Jandara’s story, pointing out that if an unknown intruder had killed Akanbi and slipped away unnoticed, why didn’t Jandara immediately alert the police? Instead, he reportedly stripped the apartment of portable belongings, even changing into Akanbi’s clothes. The murder weapon remains missing, and the case hinges on whether the jury believes Jandara’s account or sees his actions as those of a thief who turned violent.

article_content: Andrew Sable wasn’t planning to buy a new car—but the federal 'Cash for Clunkers' program gave him an offer he couldn’t ignore. 'I’d have been foolish not to take it,' said the 43-year-old insurance underwriter from North Bellmore, New York. After his son’s 1993 Jeep Grand Cherokee broke down, Sable opted to trade it in instead of repairing it. With the federal $4,500 credit and an additional $4,500 incentive from Chrysler, he walked away with $9,000 in savings, bringing the price of his new Chrysler PT Cruiser down to just $8,900 before taxes and fees. The program—officially called the Consumer Assistance to Recycle and Save Act of 2009 (CARS)—offers consumers $3,500 to $4,500 to scrap fuel-inefficient vehicles (18 mpg or lower) and replace them with cleaner, more efficient models. The old cars are destroyed to keep them off the road. Sable’s Jeep, rated at 15 mpg, was replaced with a PT Cruiser classified as an SUV at 21 mpg. Others have had similar experiences. Caroline Radtke, a freelance graphic designer in San Antonio, traded her 2000 Isuzu Trooper (15 mpg) for a diesel Volkswagen Jetta SportWagen (33 mpg). With the $4,500 federal credit, she paid under $26,000—a better car than she could’ve afforded otherwise. 'It was bad for the planet, and I was spending so much on gas,' she said. Julie Callahan, 39, of Salt Lake City, also benefited. Her 1990 Chevy C1500 pickup, with over 350,000 miles and frequent mechanical issues, earned her the same $9,000 total savings. 'Without these incentives,' she said, 'I probably wouldn’t have bought a new vehicle.' To qualify, vehicles must be under 25 years old with a clear title. The program ends November 1—or when the $1 billion fund runs out. For details, visit cars.gov or FuelEconomy.gov.

article_content: The car ferry Norman Atlantic, which caught fire in the Adriatic Sea, killing ten people and injuring dozens, was found to have serious safety flaws during an inspection just ten days earlier. The vessel, operated by Greek shipping company Anek Lines, was examined by the international maritime authority Paris MoU earlier this month and found to have faulty fire doors, insufficient life rafts, and poor emergency lighting. Emergency evacuation procedures were also criticized, raising serious questions about whether the tragedy could have been prevented. Details of the Norman Atlantic’s 'grave failings' in fire safety were published on Greek and Italian websites, citing an inspection by Paris MoU officials on December 19. Six deficiencies were identified related to emergency lighting, fire doors, and life-saving appliances that failed to meet international safety standards. Authorities reportedly gave Anek Lines 15 days to correct these issues, but it remains unclear whether any fixes were made before the ferry departed Patras, Greece, for Ancona, Italy. Trade unions have condemned Anek Lines and Italian shipowner Visemar Navigation Ltd, accusing them of cutting corners to boost profits. A joint statement from four Greek shipping unions stated: 'Once again, it is proven that shipowners’ pursuit of profit overrides the necessary measures for the protection of human life at sea.' Carlo Visentini, owner of Visemar, countered that his company actively assisted rescue operations and helped save hundreds of lives. In Bari, Italy, where many survivors were treated, Judge Giuseppe Volpe launched an investigation into the cause of the disaster, potentially leading to charges of 'culpable shipwreck.' Investigators are examining whether the fire originated in one of the lorries carrying olive oil—a highly flammable cargo—or if the cargo merely intensified an existing blaze. Confusion persists over the number of people on board. The original manifest listed 478 passengers and crew; 427 have been accounted for as rescued, including all 56 crew members. Italian Transport Minister Maurizio Lupi noted it was premature to confirm missing persons, suggesting some passengers may have reserved tickets but never boarded, while others may have traveled without documentation. Specialist Italian coast guard teams continue searching the burning wreck amid heavy rain, supported by five Greek helicopters, a Greek frigate, and another vessel.

article_content: Workplace advocates are urging employers to offer confidential alcohol screening to staff, warning that nearly one in four British workers drinks at levels that endanger their health and cost the economy billions annually. According to Don Shenker of the Alcohol Health Network, many employees are unaware of just how much they’re consuming—until they take the AUDIT, a simple questionnaire developed by the World Health Organization. The test, which asks about drinking frequency, quantity, and emotional consequences like guilt or regret, categorizes responses into four risk levels—from low to possible dependence. Shenker says those scoring in the highest bracket should receive immediate, supportive guidance, not punishment. He emphasizes that offering these tools quietly at work—through leaflets or one-on-one chats—can help people recognize risks before they spiral. While UK workplaces have long treated alcohol as part of unwinding after hours, Shenker argues that proactive prevention saves far more money than dealing with addiction later. Employers, he notes, aren’t just helping individuals—they’re reducing absenteeism, boosting productivity, and lessening broader societal burdens. And while heavy drinking could lead to job loss, the real goal isn’t discipline—it’s support.

article_content: In the past few months, Pippa Middleton has stayed busy—writing columns for Vanity Fair and The Telegraph, collaborating with Waitrose, and celebrating the christening of her nephew, Prince George. Yet amid it all, she still made time for a quiet walk through London on a chilly Friday. Dressed warmly against the winter breeze, she wore a £225 Max Studio houndstooth jacket paired with simple jeans and knee-high brown suede boots—a quintessential Chelsea look. Completing the outfit was a £475 burgundy leather and black calf hair Milan tote from Milli Millu, a rising London-based label favored by the city’s fashion-conscious community. During her stroll, Pippa paused to visit Chelsea Framers, possibly searching for the perfect frame to display a photo of Prince George. Earlier that month, on October 23, she attended the prince’s christening alongside her parents and senior royals—including the Queen and Prince Harry. For the occasion, she chose a £750 cream coat by Susannah Fashion, embodying understated elegance. Since bursting into the public eye at the 2011 Royal Wedding, Pippa has become a recognized fashion figure. Her signature Modalu Pippa bag remains a favorite, though she’s increasingly seen with pieces from Milli Millu, Alice Temperley, Issa, and American designer Misha Nonoo. article_content: The coalition was riven by bitter infighting over green taxes last night after Prime Minister David Cameron ordered a review aimed at curbing rising energy bills. Green taxes have been blamed for pushing energy prices to record levels, but the Prime Minister’s move faced fierce opposition from the Liberal Democrats, who insist the government’s green energy targets are non-negotiable. Business Secretary Vince Cable warned that attempting to lower energy bills in the short term by dismantling environmental policies would be 'short-sighted and foolish.' However, Downing Street maintained that including green energy subsidies in a broader review of measures to ease financial pressure on households was both reasonable and necessary. When asked if the government planned to review green taxes, Cameron’s official spokesperson said: 'You would expect us, when families’ budgets are under pressure, to look at whether more can be done to help them. That’s what the government will be doing.' The review is expected to focus on the £1.3 billion annual Energy Companies Obligation (Eco) scheme — a levy on energy firms used to fund home insulation for low-income households, which industry groups claim adds £100 per year to consumer bills. Other levies, including subsidies for wind farms and the carbon price floor — projected to raise £1 billion annually — may also be reconsidered. Cameron stated this week that he does not want costly subsidies for renewable energy to continue 'a minute longer than is necessary.' Chancellor George Osborne is also advocating for reforms to green subsidies and taxes to alleviate energy costs. Pressure has intensified since Labour leader Ed Miliband pledged to freeze energy bills for 20 months if Labour wins the 2015 election — despite having acknowledged in 2009, as Energy Minister, that the green taxes he introduced would inevitably raise energy prices. Cameron dismissed the pledge as a 'con,' but ministers fear its simplicity could resonate with voters struggling with soaring bills. Some Conservative ministers are urging the party to campaign on scrapping, weakening, or delaying green policies to reduce energy costs. Osborne aims for progress before his December economic statement, but major changes are likely to be blocked by strong Liberal Democrat resistance. 'The Tories can say what they want, but we will not back down on this,' a Lib Dem source said. The Eco scheme funds insulation for households defined as being in fuel poverty — those spending more than 10% of income on heating. While the cost is passed on to all consumers, Lib Dems argue it reduces bills over time. 'We’re not just talking about energy prices — we’re talking about bills,' one source noted. 'Insulating homes lowers bills in the long run.' Cable acknowledged an ongoing internal debate but reaffirmed the Lib Dems’ stance: 'If you take a long-term view of shifting Britain’s economy toward a less polluting, lower-carbon system, you must provide incentives. Renewable energy costs will fall over time.' The dispute follows SSE’s controversial announcement of an 8.2% price hike this winter, raising average dual-fuel bills to £1,465 — the highest ever recorded. Other energy firms are expected to follow. Energy Minister Michael Fallon urged customers to switch providers, but SSE CEO Alistair Phillips-Davies argued that continuing to prioritize green policies over cheaper fossil fuels will lead to further price increases.

እንዲህ አለፎታል፡ “የቤቶች የገንዘብ ቅርንጫፍ በጊዜው የሚያሳዝ ከሆነ፣ ለመረዳት የሚችል ሁሉ እንድንመለከት እንደሚጠይቅ እንደሚያስባ ነው። እሱ የመንግስት ስራ ነው።” የማስታወቂያው ከ የእንስሳት እንቅስቃሴ ስርዓት (Eco) የሚከተለው እንደሆነ ነው፣ ይህም ከመንግስት እንስሳት እንቅስቃሴ ስርዓት ከሚያስገቡት ነው። ካሜሩ የአሁን እንደሚገለጽ የአካላዊ እንቅስቃሴ ዘላቂዎች ከሚያስፈልግ ጊዜ በላይ አይቆይም ይላል። የፋይናንስ አስተዳደር ጆርጅ ኦስቦርን እንዲሁም የአካላዊ እንቅስቃሴ ዘላቂዎችን ለመቀነስ እንደሚሞክር ነው። የግለሰብ የአካላዊ ግንኙነቶች ዘላቂዎች በ2009 ዓ.ም. የመብራት ሚኒስቴር እንደሆነ የተገለጸው እንደ article_content: Passenger aircraft may fly in tight formation—like birds in a flock—by the latter half of this century, according to a bold new vision from Airbus, one of the world’s leading aircraft manufacturers. The European aerospace giant envisions formation flying becoming operational on high-traffic routes from 2050 onward. This approach, combined with steeper eco-climbs during takeoff and quiet glides during landing, could dramatically reduce noise and carbon emissions. Computer-generated simulations show futuristic Airbus planes flying in coordinated patterns. The company believes these concepts could become reality within the next few decades. By mid-century, flights across Europe and the United States could be, on average, 13 minutes shorter. This efficiency could save approximately nine million tonnes of fuel annually, while avoiding over 28 million tonnes of CO2 emissions and preserving five million flying hours. Future aircraft would be capable of 'self-organizing,' dynamically choosing the most efficient and environmentally sustainable routes in real time. Charles Champion, Airbus’s Executive Vice President for Engineering, stated: 'Our engineers are encouraged to think boldly and develop disruptive ideas that help our industry meet the ambitious 2050 sustainability targets we’ve committed to. Achieving these goals requires not only smarter aircraft design but also optimizing the entire airspace environment.' These innovations form the core of Airbus’s 'Future by Airbus: Smarter Skies' initiative, which reimagines not just what we fly—but how we fly in 2050 and beyond. The vision also includes low-emission ground operations at airports of the future.

article_content: In 'My Fair Lady', Eliza Doolittle transforms from a flower seller into a refined lady under the guidance of Professor Higgins. But in today’s political theater, Sarah Palin has flipped that script. Rather than being shaped by others, she’s become the one shaping the game. What started as a surprise vice-presidential pick in 2008 quickly evolved into something much bigger — a platform from which she could elevate others, redefine conservative politics, and stay permanently in the spotlight. Palin didn’t wait for permission to matter. She leaned into her identity as an outsider — not as a weakness, but as a superpower. By aligning with the grassroots energy of the Tea Party, she tapped into a wave of discontent that mainstream politicians couldn’t ignore. Her endorsements weren’t just appearances; they were game-changers. When she campaigned for Michele Bachmann in 2010, Bachmann’s national profile exploded. Rick Perry called her endorsement the most powerful in the Republican universe. Even John McCain, her former running mate, relied on her to revive his Senate race. And it wasn’t just allies — even rivals couldn’t help but praise her. Jon Huntsman, nominating her at the 2008 RNC, shouted over a roaring crowd: 'We are looking for Sarah.' Newt Gingrich declared she had a better resume than Barack Obama. Mitt Romney admitted she energized the base. These weren’t offhand comments — they were televised, recorded, and now form part of Palin’s unshakable legacy. Today, she doesn’t need to run for president to be a force in the race. She’s already written the script. All she has to do is press play. Her power lies not in office, but in influence — in the ability to make others shine, and in the fact that everyone who once praised her is now stuck with their own words. Whether she runs or not, Sarah Palin isn’t just a player in the game — she’s the entire production.

article_content: A father who missed the births of his first two children due to medical issues and a fear of blood has successfully delivered his third son at home. Steve Denyer, 37, a mechanic from Lancing, West Sussex, was absent during the birth of his first child, Mason, now five, after being treated for appendicitis. When his second son, Frazer, now three, was born, Steve fainted upon seeing blood. But when his wife Kirsty, 35, went into labor unexpectedly at home, Steve overcame his fears to assist in the delivery of their third son, Ollie Junior. He was asleep when Kirsty woke with back pain, went to the bathroom, and then her water broke. She called out, and Steve, still half-asleep, rushed to her side — only to see the baby’s head emerging. He immediately called emergency services. The dispatcher calmly guided him through the next steps, asking if he’d delivered a baby before. 'No,' he replied. For 30 minutes, Steve followed the dispatcher’s instructions: wiping the newborn’s face from nose to mouth — at which point the baby cried. 'That’s exactly what I wanted to hear,' the dispatcher said. Steve later described feeling overwhelming relief. Paramedics arrived shortly after 7 a.m., taking over to complete the birth. Ollie Junior weighed 8 pounds, 12 ounces. 'They were brilliant,' Steve said. 'I’d done most of it already — they just confirmed everything was fine.' Steve and Kirsty Denyer are now parents to three boys: Mason, Frazer, and Ollie Junior.

article_content: On her 30th birthday, Elizabeth Outram died by suicide at her home in Hackney, east London, after a night celebrating with friends at The Shard. An inquest heard she had been profoundly distressed following an encounter with law enforcement and a television crew at a TK Maxx store in Brighton, where she had swapped price tags on a leather jacket. The footage — recorded as she was escorted by police outside the store — was captured for a documentary, and she feared it might be broadcast nationally, deepening her existing social anxiety. Her sister, Alexandra, testified that Elizabeth had been persistently contacted by Renegade Pictures after the incident, despite explicitly asking them to cease communication and revealing she was undergoing psychiatric treatment. The production company reportedly ignored these requests and never reached out to family members, even though they held Alexandra’s contact information. Alexandra stressed that Elizabeth’s mental health had stabilized before the incident but deteriorated sharply afterward, particularly after being denied longer-term medication and compelled to attend court during a vulnerable time. In August of the prior year, Elizabeth had attempted suicide ahead of her scheduled court date. Her sister expressed bewilderment at the lack of intervention from mental health services, noting that Elizabeth’s history of severe illness and prior suicide attempts should have triggered additional safeguards. Coroner Mary Elizabeth Hassell concluded that although Elizabeth had strong familial support and was showing signs of improvement, the trauma of public exposure and absence of compassionate care proved too much to bear. Renegade Pictures later clarified that no footage from inside the shop was used, they never contacted Elizabeth directly, and she would not appear in the final program. Still, the emotional damage had already taken hold.

article_content: Leicester City have initiated talks with Argentine midfielder Esteban Cambiasso, a free agent following his departure from Inter Milan. The 33-year-old, who will turn 34 later this month, is set to meet with manager Nigel Pearson to discuss his fitness before any contract agreement is reached. With nearly 500 senior club appearances and over 50 international caps for Argentina, Cambiasso brings significant experience to the table. He is also being pursued by West Ham United, Aston Villa, and Valencia, but is reportedly seeking a two-year deal — a prospect that could stretch Leicester’s wage budget. Cambiasso, known for his midfield mastery, notably scored against Chelsea in a memorable 2010 Champions League encounter.

article_content: Mauricio Pochettino has stated he will not name Tottenham’s new captain until the summer transfer window closes. The armband is now vacant following Michael Dawson’s move to Hull City, after 324 appearances over nine years at the club. So far this season, Younes Kaboul has led the team out in Premier League matches, while Hugo Lloris captained Spurs in the first leg of their Europa League play-off against AEL Limassol last week. Pochettino is taking his time, saying, 'We will decide about the captain in the next few days — when the transfer window closes. It’s important that we have many leaders in the group. It’s been Younes and Hugo, and maybe Hugo tomorrow, or another player.' Although he declined to comment on the imminent signing of Sevilla centre-back Federico Fazio, Pochettino defended the decision to let Dawson go: 'We decided it was good for him and good for us. I needed to make a decision as a manager. The past is the past. Football is about the present. I worked with Michael for two months and wish him all the best. We recognize what he did for this club — he’s an unbelievable man and a vital player for Tottenham over the last decade.' Lloris also paid tribute: 'Michael was an example for everyone — a top guy and a gentleman. He always brought the team together and did great things for the club. It’s never easy to see a teammate leave, but this is football life. We all wish him the best. He’s an open, honest man who served as captain well.' Tottenham continue preparations for the return leg against AEL Limassol, with Sandro and Vlad Chiriches training ahead of Thursday’s match.

article_content: According to CNN, former Fulham manager Felix Magath sparked debate when he suggested using Quark — a type of soft, unripened cheese — as a topical treatment for defender Brede Hangeland’s knee injury. While widely reported as a 'cheese cure,' Magath clarified he recommended it only as a traditional method to reduce inflammation, not as a replacement for medical care. He emphasized that he would never override a doctor’s advice and that the story had been exaggerated. Magath, known for his unorthodox coaching methods, pointed out that he was merely referencing an old folk remedy. His comments echo those of American skier Lindsey Vonn, who in 2010 used Austrian cheese wrapped around her shin to ease inflammation before the Vancouver Winter Olympics. Vonn credited the method with aiding her recovery and eventual Olympic gold medal win. Though unconventional, such remedies occasionally appear in elite sports, often as complementary practices alongside professional medical treatment.

article_content: He’s not exactly known for his pro-democracy views — yet here’s North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, flashing a victory sign to student activists on the streets of Hong Kong. And there he is again, standing in front of a wall covered in messages supporting protesters occupying part of the city’s financial Admiralty district. Except, of course, it’s not really Kim Jong-un. It’s Howard, a 35-year-old Hong Kong-born Australian musician — and an uncanny lookalike. ‘I don’t really have to do anything to create awareness. Just my presence,’ Howard said. Charging HK$5,000 (£400) for party appearances, he says being a Kim doppelgänger is both amusing and politically meaningful — hoping to spark dialogue about North Korea’s human rights record. Howard became the world’s first professional Kim Jong-un lookalike last year, and since Kim rose to power in 2011, he’s endured countless jokes about his resemblance. He attributes his transformation to simple observation: ‘The key to becoming Kim is to always look unhappy and dissatisfied. That’s his trademark.’ Though he’s slightly taller, thinner, and has bushier eyebrows than Kim, Howard has perfected the dictator’s signature stern smile, stiff posture, and even his recent limp. He often wears a baseball cap and sunglasses to avoid attention during his daily life. His impersonation began accidentally in April 2012, when a photo of him dressed as Kim went viral on Facebook. He quickly launched a social media page offering his services — and received numerous requests. He later appeared in a controversial Israeli burger ad threatening to nuke America, and was once approached to collaborate with Dennis Rodman on a pistachio commercial — though visa issues canceled it. Howard says maintaining his look is easy: ‘All I have to do is eat — and eat some more.’ He finds joy in unsettling people: ‘They don’t expect to see this notorious dictator walking their streets.’ But he adds, ‘It’s always nice to go back and just be myself at the end of the day.’ His family, long supportive of his music career, now find his impersonation hilarious — and even proud. ‘They think I’ve got guts to play an evil dictator,’ he said. Meanwhile, Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement continues. Since September 28, protesters have occupied major streets in three districts after police used tear gas to disperse demonstrators rallying near government headquarters. Beijing has mandated that a committee screen candidates for Hong Kong’s 2017 chief executive election — a move widely condemned as a sham. Protesters demand the right to nominate their own candidates. To mark one month of protest, demonstrators held an evening rally featuring the unfurling of umbrellas — a symbol of resistance — followed by an 87-second silence, one second for each tear gas canister fired by police. Student leaders recently abandoned a planned street referendum after admitting they failed to properly consult the public, raising concerns about movement cohesion.

article_content: Two male nurses in Uruguay face murder charges after allegedly killing at least 16 patients across two hospitals in the nation’s capital, Montevideo. According to Judge Rolando Vomero, one nurse has been charged with five counts of aggravated homicide, and the other with 11. Authorities believe the two acted independently. A woman is also being charged as an accomplice in one of the killings. The nurses, aged 39 and 46, reportedly confessed that they killed patients to end their suffering. Their attorneys argue the acts were motivated by compassion, not malice. 'My client is fully aware of his actions and confessed to the judge and prosecutor,' said attorney Inés Massiotti. 'His defense is that he acted out of mercy,' she added. However, not all victims were terminally ill. Interior Minister Eduardo Bonomi noted that one patient had received a discharge order the day before their death. The alleged killings occurred at Maciel and La Espanola hospitals. One nurse worked in neurosurgery at La Espanola; the other worked in both neurosurgery at La Espanola and cardiology at Maciel. Police began investigating after receiving a tip from a Maciel hospital employee. A recent death provided sufficient evidence for arrests. Authorities believe the victims were killed either by morphine overdose or by injecting air into their bloodstream. The Uruguayan government has established an office to support the families of the victims, according to Health Minister Jorge Venegas.

article_content: Dr. Anthony Seldon, head of the prestigious Wellington College in Berkshire, has proposed a bold plan to reduce educational inequality in the UK. He suggests that families earning more than £80,000 annually should contribute toward the cost of sending their children to oversubscribed state schools — with fees rising as income increases. Those earning over £200,000 could be asked to pay up to £20,000 per year for secondary school and £15,000 for primary, matching the cost of elite private education. The funds raised would directly support state schools by hiring more teachers and reducing class sizes. Seldon also urges private schools to reserve 25% of their places for children from low-income backgrounds. He argues that the current system lets affluent families secure spots in top state schools by buying homes in high-demand catchment areas or paying for tutoring, effectively locking out less privileged children. Meanwhile, research from Lloyds Bank shows that homes near the UK’s best state schools carry price premiums averaging £31,500 — in some cases, like the Henrietta Barnett School in Barnet, house prices are 87% higher than surrounding areas. Similar patterns appear in villages like Whissendine and Marton, where property values surge simply due to proximity to highly rated schools. Seldon believes this is unjust: if parents can afford to game the system through property speculation and private tuition, they should help fund the public system instead of letting estate agents and tutors profit. He emphasizes that social mobility has stalled, and this reform is necessary to restore fairness and opportunity.

article_content: Former Cuban president Fidel Castro celebrated his 88th birthday across Cuba—with officials marking the occasion with tributes in state media, a concert by the Cuban duo Buena Fe, a photo exhibition at Havana’s José Martí Memorial, and the inauguration of a restored version of his birthplace. Despite having survived over 600 alleged assassination attempts—many attributed to the CIA during the Cold War—Castro has remained a towering, if reclusive, figure in Cuban history. Many Cuban exiles in Florida condemn him as a dictator who crushed civil liberties with an iron fist, while in Cuba, he is still honored as a champion of equality and social justice who defied the United States for five decades. Fabian Escalante, Castro’s former head of security, claimed there were 638 CIA plots against him, including infamous schemes like exploding cigars and poisoned fountain pens—most concentrated in the early 1960s under Operation Mongoose. Some of these plots were detailed in a 2006 Channel 4 documentary titled '638 Ways to Kill Castro.' One well-known attempt involved Castro’s former mistress, Marita Lorenz, who was allegedly tasked with feeding him poisoned capsules. She later said Castro confronted her with a gun and urged her to kill him—which she refused to do. Castro ruled Cuba from 1959 until 2008, when he stepped down after a serious illness and transferred power to his younger brother, Raúl Castro. In recent years, Castro has made few public appearances. His last major one was a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin. A new book, 'La Vie Cachée de Fidel Castro' (Fidel Castro’s Hidden Life), written by former bodyguard Juan Reinaldo Sánchez, claims Castro lived in luxury on a private island, Cayo Piedra, south of the Bay of Pigs—a paradise complete with turtle and dolphin farms—contrary to his publicly promoted image of austere communist simplicity. Sánchez, who now lives in the United States, asserts that most Cubans were unaware of their leader’s opulent lifestyle, which sharply contrasted with the economic hardships faced by ordinary citizens. The Communist Party newspaper Granma declared, 'Paying homage to Fidel is a great party,' reflecting the official stance of celebration. Castro did not make a public appearance on his actual birthday in 2015, continuing his pattern of seclusion since stepping down from office.
translated_content: የキュባ የቀደመ ፕሬዚደንት ፊደል ካስትሮ የ88ኛው የተሰለፈ ቀን በኩላቸው በキュባ ላይ ተጠራጥሮ ነበር—የመንግስት መማሪያዎች በአገር መስመር ውስጥ የሚታዩ ምድር ጥበቦች፣ በሐቪና የሆነ የሆነ አዲስ ማህበረሰብ ውስጥ የቡዕና ፋ የተሰራ አካባቢ እና የተደረገ ቤት ማስተካከያ በሚካሔድ አካባቢ ላይ ተመልካች ነበር። የCIA የተጠናከረ የ638 የሞት እርምጃዎች ስለተጠናከሩ ነበር፣ ካስትሮ በキュባ ሳህል ላይ በጣም አስቸጋሪ እና በተደጋጋሚ አስተዋፅኦ ያለው ነገር ነበር። በፍሎሪዳ ውስጥ የሚኖሩ ከキュባ የሚመለሰው ሰዎች እርሱን በእጅ ላይ ምክር አድርጎ የሰብዓዊ ክፍል ስርዓት ሰብሳዊ ማስወገድ የሚያደርግ የ dictatorship አመለካከት ናቸው፣ ነገር ግን በキュባ ውስጥ እርሱ በመስክ እና በማስተዋፅኦ ምክር ለአንድ ዘመን ሰፊ አስተዋፅኦ ነበር። Fabian Escalante, ካስትሮ የቀደመ የአስተዋፅኦ አመለካከት, 638 የCIA የሞት እርምጃዎች ስለተጠናከሩ ነበር፣ የተወሰነ የሞት እርምጃዎች እንደ አስተማሪ ሞርጌ እና የተከተለ የ墨水 ቁልፍ ከ1960 ዎች ጀምሮ ከOperation Mongoose ጋር በተያያዘ ነበር። እነዚህ እርምጃዎች ከ2006 የChannel 4 የድርሻ ትርጉም የ ‘638 Ways to Kill Castro’ የተባለ የተጠራጥሮ ውስጥ ተገልጿል። ከተወሰነ እርምጃ ውስጥ የካስትሮ የቀደመ ልጅ ማሪታ ሊርንዝ በሚመለስ የተሰራ ነበር። እርሱ እንደ እርሱ የተሰራ የአጠቃላይ እርምጃ ነበር። ከ1959 እስከ 2008 ድረስ በキュባ የሥልጣን አለመ ካስትሮ በቅርብ አልደረገውም እና ከዚያ በኋላ የወለድ ምክር ከወልድ አካባቢ እስከ እርሱ የልደት ቤት ማስተካከያ ድረስ አስተዋፅኦ ነበር። በቅርብ ዘመኖች ካስትሮ በጣም በትንሽ የተገለጸ ነበር። የወደፊቱ የተሰራ ምክር በሮሺያ ፕሬዚደንት ወላዲሚር ፖቲን ጋር አንድ ተገናኝ ነበር። በአዲስ የተዘረዘረ የ‘La Vie Cachée de Fidel Castro’ የተባለ የተዘረዘረ መጽሐፍ የሚያሳይ ካስትሮ በየወለድ ምክር የተገለጸ የአዲስ አገር ከተማ ውስጥ እንደ ምስጢር የተሰራ ነበር፣ ይህም የምስጢር የጥርስ እና የዶልፊን አገር ያለው ነበር። የእርሱ የቀደመ አስተዋፅኦ የጁአን ሮናልዶ ሳንቺ የሚያሳይ ካስትሮ በአሜሪካ ውስጥ ነበር እና የキュባ ሰዎች የአስተዋፅኦ ምክር ለአስተዋፅኦ ስርዓት የተሰራ ነበር። የኮሚኒስት ፓርቲ የግራማ የአገር ምስጢር የሚያሳይ ካስትሮ ለማስተዋፅኦ አስተዋፅኦ ነበር። ከ1959 እስከ 2008 ድረስ በキュባ የሥልጣን አለመ ካስትሮ በቅርብ አልደረገውም እና ከዚያ በኋላ የወለድ ምክር ከወልድ አካባቢ እስከ እርሱ የልደት ቤት ማስተካከያ ድረስ አስተዋፅኦ ነበር።

article_content: As drug-related violence surges across the border in Mexico, U.S. officials are scrambling to respond to growing fears that the chaos could reach American soil. Cities like Ciudad Juárez have become battlegrounds, with over 1,800 people killed since early 2008 — a death toll far exceeding any U.S. city. In response, Congress is preparing to question Homeland Security leaders about how to stop the flow of weapons from U.S. gun shops — many located just miles from the border — into the hands of Mexican cartels. Rep. Loretta Sanchez, who chairs the key House committee overseeing border issues, warned that what was once a localized problem is now deeply intertwined with U.S. economic and security interests. 'It’s not just about fencing off the border,' she said. 'We need to understand how poverty, trade, and illegal arms sales feed this cycle.' She urged lawmakers to consider banning the sale of assault-style rifles near the border and strengthening oversight of licensed dealers. Vice President Joe Biden highlighted the staggering human cost: nearly 7,000 drug-related homicides in Mexico since last year alone. He linked the crisis to the appointment of Gil Kerlikowske as the new White House drug czar, whose mandate includes shaping a unified Southwest border strategy. Meanwhile, the U.S. government is exploring ways to assist Mexico without turning the border into a militarized zone. President Obama said he’s open to deploying the National Guard if violence escalates — but stressed that any move must be part of a broader, collaborative plan with President Calderón. Intelligence sharing, drone surveillance, and forensic training are among the non-combat tools under discussion. Travel warnings from the U.S. State Department and allies like Canada and Germany reflect rising global unease. In Jalisco, five severed heads found in refrigerators underscored the brutality now routine in parts of Mexico. As cartels battle for control of lucrative U.S. drug markets, experts warn the violence won’t stay contained — and neither should the U.S. response.

article_content: David Mellor, a 62-year-old jeweller, bravely confronted two armed thieves who smashed their way into his Andover shop to steal thousands of pounds worth of luxury watches. On September 8, Tom White, 26, used a claw hammer to shatter the glass displays, grabbing multiple high-value timepieces including a Rolex, a Cartier 18-carat white gold watch, and a Cartier Roadster, while his accomplice, Luke Peverall, 24, waited on a motorbike nearby. Mellor, despite having undergone hip and knee replacements, rushed to stop them, seizing the stolen bag—but was thrown to the pavement in the struggle. The pair fled on the bike, but were later arrested in Reading after police traced a phone left behind at the scene. Both pleaded guilty to conspiracy to rob and were sentenced to five years in prison at Winchester Crown Court. Judge Keith Cutler emphasized that such crimes carry inherent dangers, noting Mellor’s injuries as a direct consequence of their actions. The attack left Mellor and his staff deeply shaken. ‘Every time a motorbike passes, my heart stops,’ Mellor said. In response, full-time security has been installed across all three of his jewellery stores.

article_content: Raleigh, North Carolina (CNN) — Washington no longer holds a monopoly on bitter partisanship. Much of the nation’s political division has spread to statehouses across the country. The weekly demonstrations outside the North Carolina legislature, known as 'Moral Mondays,' are among the most visible examples. For three months, liberal activists have gathered each Monday outside the GOP-controlled statehouse to protest what they describe as an aggressive and rapid conservative agenda. One protest sign read: 'First the Great Recession. Now the Great Regression.' 'It’s about exposing what’s immoral and extreme,' said Rev. William Barber II, a key leader of the Moral Monday movement. Republican leaders routinely ignore the demonstrators and their signs. Since gaining control of both the legislature and the governor’s office for the first time in over a century, GOP lawmakers have pushed through a series of conservative policies. This year, Governor Pat McCrory and Republican legislators cut unemployment benefits, rejected Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act, and introduced changes to voting laws—prompting strong backlash from Democrats. On the same day as the latest Moral Monday protest, McCrory announced a deal to lower state personal income and corporate taxes. Democrats viewed this as another item checked off the Tea Party agenda. In an interview with CNN, McCrory described the changes as 'pragmatic, systematic reforms' designed to make North Carolina more economically competitive. He dismissed claims that he is advancing a purely conservative agenda. 'I’ve stepped on toes—in my first six months in office—of the right, the left, and the media,' McCrory said. 'Maybe that means I’m doing something right.' Democrats, who currently hold no power to pass, sign, or block legislation—something they say hasn’t happened in living memory—feel targeted. They accuse McCrory and Republicans of trying to 'turn back the clock.' 'Overall, there’s a movement—what we’d call it—backward,' said Democratic State Senator Ben Clark. McCrory points to his 14-year tenure as mayor of Charlotte as evidence he can collaborate across party lines. But Democratic lawmakers are still waiting for that bipartisanship to materialize in Raleigh. For progressives in a state that helped elect President Barack Obama in 2008, protest remains their primary tool. At this week’s gathering, thousands demonstrated outside the legislature, and hundreds entered the building for a coordinated act of civil disobedience, resulting in dozens of arrests. Gayle Ruedi, a veteran protester arrested in May, returned despite having her first court date this week. 'What they did with unemployment is wrong. What they did with Medicaid is wrong. And what they’re doing with abortion is wrong,' she said. Last week, the North Carolina House approved new regulations governing abortion providers. McCrory has signaled he will sign them into law—a move Democrats say violates his campaign pledge to avoid new abortion restrictions. 'Absolutely not,' McCrory insisted. 'These are just necessary legal updates to existing rules. That’s a promise kept.' The surge in partisan conflict challenges North Carolina’s longstanding image as a business-friendly, moderate state. 'I think there are people everywhere who say this level of disagreement doesn’t help,' said Dr. Andy Taylor, a political science professor at North Carolina State University. With the state’s unemployment rate at 8.8%, McCrory argues North Carolina needed bold new direction. 'They’re fighting to preserve the status quo,' he said of the protesters. Taylor notes that Raleigh’s political turmoil mirrors similar battles in Texas and Wisconsin, where Republican governors have also advanced contentious abortion restrictions. As in Austin and Madison, liberal protests have had minimal impact on legislative outcomes. Leaders of the Moral Monday movement say they plan to continue weekly rallies even after the legislative session ends—knowing their direct influence on current laws is limited. Their goal: mobilize voters for next year’s elections. 'The one thing they don’t want to see is all of us coming together,' Barber said.

article_content: (CNN) — Is the dome doomed? Voters may have delivered the final blow to the Astrodome, Houston’s iconic and once groundbreaking stadium. While it’s too soon to write its obituary, the rejection of the bond initiative Tuesday night has tilted the scales heavily toward demolition. Harris County residents were asked whether to approve $217 million in bonds to transform the aging structure into a massive exhibition and events venue. The county owns the Astrodome, and commissioners had warned that failure to pass the measure would leave demolition as the only remaining option. The proposition was defeated by a 53% to 47% margin. Harris County Judge Ed Emmett’s spokesperson, Joe Stinebaker, stated that with no viable public or private alternatives, demolition appears inevitable. However, no formal decision has been made yet. The county commission has not added demolition to its agenda, but it could be considered as early as next Tuesday. A majority of commissioners previously indicated they would support demolition if the bond failed. Whether they voted yes or no, Houstonians share a deep nostalgia for the stadium. Opened in 1965, it was the world’s first domed stadium and celebrated as a marvel of engineering. It served as the longtime home of the Houston Astros and Houston Oilers, and hosted rodeos, concerts, and major events. Stephen Chmaitelli, 38, recalls being dropped off at the Astrodome as a child with friends to catch a game before heading to the now-closed Astroworld theme park. 'It was a fun way to spend summer days,' he said. 'There are just so many memories there.' He voted in favor of saving it, inspired by renderings showing a modernized space larger than the city’s convention center — one that preserves the dome’s spirit while upgrading its function. Chmaitelli argued the renovation made economic sense: acquiring comparable land today and building something similar would cost far more. Bowen Shepard, 32, a Houston native, agreed the Astrodome was a source of civic pride — but voted against the bond. He cited years of decay and the structure’s awkward contrast beside the modern Reliant Stadium. 'Everything has its time,' he said. 'And every time comes to an end.' Months before the vote, even before it was officially announced, the National Trust for Historic Preservation placed the Astrodome on its annual list of '11 Most Endangered Historical Places.' On the same day the revitalization plan was unveiled, the Trust also named it one of 35 'national treasures,' committing resources to its preservation. 'We’re disappointed this morning,' said Beth Wiedower, a senior field officer for the Trust. 'I think the outcome reflects more confusion around the Astrodome’s future over the past few years than a rejection of its value.' For the past five years, the Astrodome has sat largely vacant. Electricity and water remain on, but it’s primarily used for storage. The county estimates annual maintenance costs between $2 million and $3 million. Though several private proposals have surfaced over the years, none secured funding. Wiedower believes many voters misunderstood the vote as merely one step in a longer process — not a final decision. Now, with the door closing, she predicts widespread regret among Houstonians. 'If the city changes its mind,' Stinebaker noted, 'the only path forward may be a private-sector 'white knight' stepping in with a funded plan.'

article_content: For over four decades, a 1959 Morris Mini Minor Saloon sat forgotten in a damp barn near Bicester, its once-cherry-red paint faded under layers of rust. Now, this humble relic — the 15th oldest known Mini in existence and the 529th ever made — is headed to auction. Originally purchased by a local man 54 years ago, the car suffered a front-end collision not long after, prompting him to park it for repairs that never happened. Despite its weathered state, the vehicle still carries its original engine and has logged just under 47,000 miles. Its rediscovery came last month after the owner’s family cleared out the barn following his passing. Experts at Bonhams believe it will attract serious attention from classic car lovers eager to restore a piece of motoring history. The Mini, designed by Sir Alec Issigonis, transformed British automotive design with its compact, front-wheel-drive layout and space-efficient engineering. Introduced as the Morris Mini Minor and Austin Seven before becoming its own brand in 1969, the Mini became a symbol of 1960s innovation, with more than 5,000 units rolling off production lines weekly at its peak. Issigonis, a Greek-British engineer, championed efficiency and clever packaging — principles that made the Mini not just practical, but revolutionary. Today, collectors still prize these early models for their purity and heritage. With the eighth-oldest Mini having sold for £40,000 in 2011, this one could easily command a similar sum — especially for someone ready to take on a rewarding restoration challenge.

article_content: In Mohali, India, a team of over 200 workers completed a 10-story building—dubbed Instacon—in just 48 hours, setting a national record for speed of construction. Work began at 4:30 p.m. on Thursday and concluded precisely at 4:30 p.m. on Saturday, with crews working around the clock using three cranes to assemble the 200-tonne structure, covering more than 25,000 square meters. The building, designed by I.C. Syal, a former professor at Punjab Engineering College, features a 'tube-in-tube' structural system designed to withstand extreme conditions. According to Syal, the building’s maximum deflection under simulated wind and seismic loads was just 49 millimeters—well below the government’s allowable limit of 123 millimeters for conventional buildings. He stated the structure is engineered with materials and methods intended to provide exceptional durability, with projections suggesting a service life of up to 600 years under proper maintenance. Harpal Singh, CMD of Synergy Thrislington—the Mohali-based infrastructure firm behind the project—presented a certificate from the Limca Book of Records confirming the record. While the exterior and core structure were completed on schedule, internal systems such as air conditioning, lighting, and plumbing will be installed in subsequent phases.

article_content: Two men who faced the death penalty for a 1975 murder have been released from prison after all charges against them were dismissed — following the recantation of the sole eyewitness, who admitted his testimony was fabricated. Ricky Jackson, 57, and Wiley Bridgeman, 60, were convicted of murdering businessman Harry Franks in Cleveland, Ohio, primarily based on the account of a 12-year-old boy, Eddie Vernon. Along with Bridgeman’s brother Ronnie, they were sentenced to death. After the U.S. Supreme Court effectively abolished the death penalty in 1978 (Furman v. Georgia), their sentences were commuted to life imprisonment. Ronnie Bridgeman, who later changed his name to Kwame Ajamu, was released in 2003 on unrelated grounds. On Friday, Jackson and Bridgeman walked free from Cuyahoga County Jail after prosecutors moved to dismiss the charges. Vernon, now 52, recanted his testimony in court, stating that police coerced him into giving false statements and fed him details of the crime. He also feared his parents would face prison for perjury if he withdrew his testimony. Multiple children on the bus at the time confirmed Vernon could not have seen the murder from his seat. Judge Richard McMonagle called the dismissal 'a big one,' adding, 'Life is filled with small victories.' Jackson, overwhelmed with emotion, said, 'I’m on an emotional high.' Bridgeman, who never lost hope, embraced his brother Ajamu upon release. Ajamu, who spent his 18th birthday on death row and lost several family members while incarcerated, said, 'Stick with me. You’ll be all right. I ain’t never going to let you go.' Jackson plans to celebrate with a fish dinner — his first meal out of prison. Though he spent nearly four decades behind bars, Jackson expressed no anger toward Vernon, saying, 'It took a lot of courage to do what he did.' Prosecutors acknowledged the injustice, stating, 'The state concedes the obvious.' Jackson’s sentence had actually been commuted in 1977 due to a procedural error, making his case distinct from the others.

article_content: Anna Fenninger might wish every ski race were held on December 28th — it’s clearly her lucky day. The Austrian alpine skier claimed her third consecutive victory on this date, winning the women’s giant slalom in Lienz, Austria. After trailing by just 0.02 seconds following the first run, Fenninger delivered a flawless second run to take the win. She previously won giant slaloms in Lienz in 2011 and Semmering, Austria, in 2012, both also on December 28th. Sweden’s Jessica Lindell-Vikarby finished 0.50 seconds behind, while reigning slalom champion Mikaela Shiffrin of the United States came in third, just 0.01 seconds behind Lindell-Vikarby. 'I can’t explain why I’m so successful on this day,' Fenninger told FIS, the sport’s governing body. 'It’s amazing to win again. I have wonderful memories from my first victory here, and they definitely help. I truly love Lienz and this slope.' The win propelled Fenninger into second place in the overall World Cup standings, behind Tina Weirather, who finished 17th on Saturday. It was Fenninger’s first podium in five giant slalom races this season. 'I was a bit disappointed with my recent giant slalom results,' she admitted. 'We’ve had many speed events lately, and I hadn’t trained enough for GS. I didn’t expect to win today, but I gave everything — and it paid off. Winning in front of a home crowd makes it extra special.' Lindell-Vikarby, meanwhile, extended her lead in the giant slalom discipline standings. 'I’m thrilled to be on the podium and keep the red bib,' she said. 'Last week in Val d’Isère, I finished sixth and was frustrated with my mistakes. Today felt completely different — I’m really happy.' Meanwhile, unseasonably warm weather forced organizers to cancel the scheduled men’s and women’s slalom races in Zagreb, Croatia, next week.

article_content: A Kenyan hotel worker, Ali Babitu Kololo, has been sentenced to death for his role in the 2011 kidnapping of British tourist Judith Tebbutt and the fatal shooting of her husband, David Tebbutt. Kololo, 27, was convicted of robbery with violence and kidnapping with intent to cause murder following a brutal attack by Somali pirates at the Kiwayu Safari Village in Lamu County on September 11, 2011. During the attack, the couple — both 58 and staying at the remote resort — were assaulted in their beachside cottage. David Tebbutt was shot dead as he tried to defend his wife. Judith Tebbutt was dragged onto a speedboat and taken to Somalia, where she remained captive for over six months before being freed in March 2012 after her family paid a ransom. Kololo, a former employee of the resort and a Muslim father of two, was arrested the day after the attack and remains the only person charged in connection with the incident. He admitted in court to guiding the pirates to the Tebbutts’ cottage but insisted he did so under duress, having been kidnapped by the same group earlier that night. Magistrate Johnstone Munguti dismissed Kololo’s claim of coercion, stating that evidence — including testimony from Judith Tebbutt and statements from her captors — pointed conclusively to his involvement as the sixth attacker. Although Mrs. Tebbutt could not positively identify him, one of the pirates indicated that someone left behind in Kenya was 'in big trouble,' a detail uniquely matching Kololo’s arrest. Kololo was sentenced to death for robbery with violence and seven years for kidnapping. However, Kenya has not carried out an execution since 1987 and is currently reviewing its capital punishment laws. Legal experts believe his sentence will likely be commuted to life imprisonment. Judith Tebbutt, who detailed her experience in her memoir, A Long Walk Home, believes Kololo played a critical role in enabling the attack, writing: 'Ali Babitu Kololo was not among the five men who took me off Kiwayu in a skiff. But if he is found guilty of the crime for which he stands accused then he is deeply complicit — things would not have happened as they did had the pirates not been guided around the island as they evidently were.' British Ambassador to Somalia Neil Wigan welcomed the verdict on Twitter, calling it a step toward justice. Meanwhile, Kenyan authorities continue to investigate the remaining pirates believed to be hiding in Somalia, though their capture remains unlikely.

article_content: The former country home of one of Hollywood's most iconic actresses, Vivien Leigh, has been listed for sale at £3.5 million. Tickerage Mill, located near Uckfield in East Sussex, was purchased by Leigh for £20,000 in 1961, shortly after her divorce from Laurence Olivier. She used the estate as a peaceful retreat while battling tuberculosis and depression. Following her death in 1967 at age 53, her ashes were scattered over the pond on the property. During her time there, Leigh hosted numerous prominent figures, including Laurence Olivier, Princess Margaret, John Gielgud, John Merivale — her companion in later years — and Winston Churchill. The Grade II listed five-bedroom mansion features an ancient bluebell wood, a walled garden, and a separate gardener’s cottage. Merivale, a Canadian actor, provided steadfast support during Leigh’s final years and is said to have assured Olivier he would care for her. Current owners Ken and Honor Hoggins have lived at Tickerage Mill since 2005 and have carefully preserved its historical character and Leigh’s personal touches, including her favorite white-flowering wisteria and a marble fireplace shipped from Venice. Artistic additions to the property were made by Richard Wyndham, who owned the estate in the 1920s and built an artist’s studio. Other past residents include Sir Ronald Armstrong Jones (father of Princess Margaret’s husband) and Kenneth Letts, creator of the Letts Diaries. Estate agent Sophie Wysock-Wright of Savills notes that while the Leigh connection draws significant interest, the property’s rarity as a secluded yet accessible mill house appeals to buyers seeking tranquility away from urban life.

article_content: At 75, British grandmother Paddy Jones — real name Sarah — stunned audiences on Spain’s 'Tu Si Que Vales' with a breathtaking salsa acrobática routine that left judges and viewers speechless. Once a professional dancer in her youth, she rekindled her passion for movement five years ago after losing her husband, choosing salsa not just to stay active but to rediscover joy. Onstage in Gandia, Spain, she stepped out arm-in-arm with Nico, her 35-year-old dance instructor, wearing towering heels and radiating confidence. What followed was a whirlwind of lifts, backflips from his shoulders, and a final overhead flip that brought the crowd to its feet. Videos of the performance exploded online, with comments flooding in: 'Incredible,' 'This is what resilience looks like,' 'A true inspiration.' Jones, now living quietly in Spain, says the sudden fame has been overwhelming — strangers stop her at the doctor’s office, the grocery store, even the gas station. 'I never imagined this,' she told the Stourbridge News. Her story mirrors that of Susan Boyle, the Scottish singer whose voice captivated the world and whose album 'I Dreamed a Dream' broke records in the U.S., selling over 700,000 copies in its first week. Both women defied expectations not through perfection, but through pure, unapologetic spirit.

article_content: In a quiet, dilapidated home in Dayton, Ohio, a young boy made a chilling discovery: the mummified remains of a man hanging from a belt in a closet. Authorities later revealed the body had been there since 2009—five long years unnoticed by anyone in the neighborhood. The house, covered in code violation notices for its overgrown yard, appeared completely abandoned. No one had visited, and no signs of life were visible from the outside. Inside, it was bare—no furniture, no personal items, just silence and decay. The deceased was identified as Edward Brunton, a man in his late 40s who had bought the house just months before taking his own life. Because he was estranged from family and friends—and had no ties to the community—no one missed him or reported him gone. The closet where he died acted like a natural preservation chamber: shielded from light, air, and moisture. As a result, his body dried out instead of decomposing, turning into what experts describe as a near-perfect mummy. It was only when the boy’s mother, Michelle McGrath, stepped into the room and caught a foul odor that the truth came to light. She immediately called the police. Officials found ID on the body, and Brunton’s brother, though distant, confirmed his identity. This case underscores how easily someone can vanish from sight—not because they disappeared, but because no one was paying attention.
